1.title: The labels we live by
1.brief: A cultural magazine has invited readers to submit articles for a series called 'Who do you think you are?'. Write an article in which you explore how labels such as nationality, profession or generation shape the way people see themselves, and whether we would be better off without them.
1.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para una revista cultural sobre cómo las etiquetas (nacionalidad, profesión, generación) moldean nuestra identidad y si estaríamos mejor sin ellas.
criteria: An engaging title and opening that addresses the reader directly.
Perfect and continuous aspect used for nuance (I have been wondering, I had always assumed).
At least one stative verb used dynamically (I'm being unfair, we are forever seeing ourselves as…).
Word formation with un-, dis-, -hood and -ness, and an idiom of belonging (a fish out of water, to put down roots).
1.model:
Tick the Box, Lose the Plot?

I have been filling in forms for most of my adult life, and I have only recently begun to notice how much they ask me to decide who I am. Nationality: one box. Occupation: one line. Age group: pick a bracket. Each answer seems harmless enough. Taken together, they amount to a portrait, and not always one I recognise.

Labels, of course, exist for good reasons. They help strangers make sense of one another quickly, and they can offer a genuine sense of belonging. Anyone who has felt like a fish out of water in a foreign city will know the relief of hearing their own accent across a crowded room.

The trouble begins when the label stops describing us and starts directing us. I had always assumed that being 'an engineer' was simply what I did; it was only when I lost my job that I realised how much of my selfhood I had invested in the word. For months I felt strangely disconnected, as though I had mislaid a part of myself. Generational labels are, if anything, even more slippery. Those of us lumped together as 'millennials' are forever being told what we think, usually by people who have never asked us.

Would we be better off without labels altogether? I doubt it. A world of unlabelled individuals would be a lonely place, and the urge to put down roots and name where we belong is deeply human. What we need is not the abolition of labels but a lighter grip on them. I am still an engineer, still a Colombian, still, regrettably, a millennial. But I am also being, I hope, a little more curious about the parts of me that no form has a box for.

Perhaps that is the real answer to the question 'Who do you think you are?': rather more than you have been told.

1.title: Rooted or rootless?
1.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — The value of staying put
Communities in which people remain for generations possess a form of wealth that rarely appears in economic statistics. Neighbours know one another's histories; obligations are remembered and repaid; children grow up surrounded by adults who feel some responsibility for them. Mobility, often celebrated as freedom, quietly erodes these bonds. When everyone is passing through, nobody is accountable to anyone, and the loneliness that afflicts many modern cities is the price we pay.

Text 2 — The freedom to leave
The nostalgia for rooted communities overlooks how stifling they could be. For many people, particularly women and minorities, the village that 'looked after its own' was also the village that dictated whom they could marry and what they could become. Moving away has allowed millions to reinvent themselves. Identity is not something we inherit like furniture; it is something we build, and for many the building can only begin once they have left home.
1.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre el arraigo frente a la movilidad, añadiendo tus propias ideas.
criteria: Both texts summarised accurately in your own words, without copying phrases.
A clear evaluation of each writer's argument and a reasoned personal position.
Aspect used for nuance (have long been, had been hoping) and at least one past form for distancing.
Formal, cohesive essay register with varied linking (whereas, by contrast, it could be argued).
1.model:
Both texts address the tension between belonging to a settled community and the freedom to leave it, although they reach markedly different conclusions.

The first writer argues that long-established communities offer a kind of social capital that cannot be measured in economic terms: mutual knowledge, a sense of obligation and shared responsibility for the young. In his view, the modern enthusiasm for mobility has weakened these ties, and the isolation many city-dwellers experience is a direct consequence. The point is well made, and anyone who has lived in an anonymous apartment block will recognise the loneliness he describes. However, the text presents rootedness in a rather idealised light, saying nothing about who benefits from such close-knit arrangements and who does not.

It is precisely this omission that the second writer addresses. She contends that tightly bound communities have often been oppressive, especially for those whose choices did not conform to local expectations, and that leaving has enabled countless people to shape their own identities. Her claim that identity is constructed rather than inherited is persuasive, although she perhaps underestimates how much people who move continue to draw on the communities they have left behind.

In my view, the two positions are less opposed than they first appear. Belonging and freedom are both genuine needs, and most people have been negotiating between them all their lives. The real question is whether communities can be open enough to let people leave and welcoming enough to let newcomers in. A place that manages both would, I suspect, satisfy the concerns of each writer, and it is towards such places, rather than a return to the past, that we should be working.

1.title: The accent I used to hide
1.brief: A literary magazine is publishing reflective essays under the heading 'Home in the mouth'. Write a reflective essay about a feature of the way you speak (an accent, a dialect word, a habit of speech) that you once tried to change or hide, and what it has come to mean to you.
1.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo reflexivo sobre un rasgo de tu forma de hablar (acento, palabra regional) que intentaste ocultar y lo que significa hoy para ti.
criteria: Perfect and continuous aspect used for nuance (had been hiding, have been letting).
At least one stative verb used dynamically (I was being defensive, I am seeing it differently).
A distancing or unreal past for tact or reflection (I was wondering whether…, If I were to…).
Word formation with un-, -ness or -hood, and one idiom of belonging (to find your feet, to feel at home).
1.model:
Where I Come From, Out Loud

For years I had been hiding my accent without admitting it, even to myself. When I moved from Cali to Bogotá at seventeen, I noticed that my vowels marked me out within seconds. I was convinced that people were judging my intelligence by the way I stretched my words, so I set about flattening them, rehearsing sentences in the bathroom mirror as though preparing for an audition.

It worked, after a fashion. Within two years I had stopped being asked where I was from, and I assumed that I had finally found my feet. What I had not considered was the cost. When I phoned my grandmother, I would catch myself slipping back, and she would laugh and say that I sounded like a stranger who had borrowed my voice. I was being defensive, of course, and she knew it.

The turning point came unexpectedly. A colleague, listening to me tell a story, remarked that she had always thought my way of speaking was warm. Warm! I had spent a decade treating it as a flaw. I was wondering whether she was simply being polite, but she was not; she asked me to teach her three of my regional words, and I realised how rarely anyone had wanted to learn something from me.

Since then I have been letting the accent return, unevenly and a little self-consciously. Some days it feels like an unwelcome visitor; others, like a coat I had forgotten I owned. I am seeing it now as part of my belonging rather than an obstacle to it. Childhood is not something one outgrows, and the unmistakable music of my region is, I think, one of the few things I can carry anywhere.

If I were to give my younger self a piece of advice, it would be to stop apologising. Home is not something you leave behind in your pronunciation; it persists, quietly and a little stubbornly, in the way you say your own name.

1.title: Review: a novel about coming home
1.brief: A literary supplement is running a series called 'Books that made me rethink where I belong'. Write a review of a novel, real or imagined, about migration, return or belonging. Summarise the premise without spoiling the ending, assess the author's style and say who should read it.
1.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de una novela, real o imaginada, sobre migración, regreso o pertenencia: argumento sin destripar el final, estilo y a quién se la recomiendas.
criteria: Perfect aspect used to organise the review (had expected, has been compared).
At least one stative verb used dynamically (Inés is being evasive, I was seeing the village anew).
At least one distancing past for a tentative judgement (I was hoping for…, I wondered whether…).
Word formation with dis-, un-, -ness or -hood, and an idiom of belonging (a fish out of water, to put down roots).
1.model:
Salt on the Doorstep: A Return That Refuses to Be Simple

I had expected a gentle novel about homecoming. What I found in 'Salt on the Doorstep' is something sharper and considerably less comfortable. Its protagonist, Inés, returns to a fishing village in northern Chile after twenty years abroad, intending to sell her late father's house. She has been away for so long that she is a fish out of water in her own kitchen, and the novel has been compared, not unfairly, to the work of authors who treat memory as a form of weather.

The strength of the book lies in its patience. The author does not announce Inés's disconnection; she lets us watch it accumulate in small humiliations, such as forgetting a neighbour's name or misjudging the price of bread. Inés is being evasive with everyone, including the reader, and it takes a hundred pages before we understand what she is avoiding. I was hoping for a revelation, and the actual secret is quieter than that, which I came to admire.

There are weaknesses. The middle chapters drag, and a subplot involving a disputed fishing licence feels like an unwelcome detour. The dialogue, moreover, is occasionally stiff, as if translated from another language rather than written in it. Still, the prose is lean and precise, and the closing pages, in which Inés finally decides whether to put down roots, are unexpectedly moving. I will not reveal her choice.

Who should read it? Anyone who has ever lived between two countries will recognise the restlessness the author captures so well, and readers weary of tidy narratives about belonging will welcome its honesty. It will not offer the reassurance of a happy homecoming. What it offers instead is the rarer comfort of being understood: the book suggests that neighbourhood and childhood are not places we return to, but states of mind we carry, edit and sometimes outgrow.

1.title: The question behind the question
1.brief: A newspaper's opinion page is collecting short pieces on everyday assumptions. Write an opinion article arguing for or against the habit of asking people where they are 'really' from. Consider why the question is asked, how it can sound to the listener, and what could be asked instead.
1.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de opinión sobre la costumbre de preguntar a alguien de dónde es 'realmente': por qué se hace, cómo suena y qué alternativa hay.
criteria: Perfect and continuous aspect for nuance (have been asked, had never realised).
At least two stative verbs used dynamically (he is being friendly, she is being polite).
A distancing past used for tact or reflection (I was wondering whether…).
Word formation with un-, dis-, -ness or -hood, and one idiom of belonging (to fit in, to put down roots).
1.model:
The Question Behind the Question

'No, but where are you really from?' Most people who have heard this sentence can recall the exact moment, usually after an answer that was perfectly adequate. I have been asked it for thirty years, and I had never realised how much it unsettles me until my daughter, aged seven, was asked it by a stranger in a supermarket queue.

Defenders of the question insist that it is curiosity, and I accept that most of the time it is. The person asking is rarely being hostile; he is often being friendly in an awkward way. But the word 'really' gives the game away. It suggests that my first answer, the city where I was born and have worked all my life, was somehow a dishonest one, and that my belonging needs verifying before it is granted.

Consider the effect on the listener. Those who ask rarely think of it as a test; those who answer it frequently feel examined. Every repetition adds a small reminder that she does not entirely fit in. One conversation is nothing; a lifetime of them is a quiet erosion of confidence. The weariness is cumulative, and it is invisible to those who have never been asked.

So what should we do instead? I am not suggesting that people stop being curious. I was wondering, when I began writing this, whether a simple alternative existed, and it does: wait. Ask about someone's work, their weekend or their opinion of the coffee. If they want to tell you about their grandparents' village, they will, usually within ten minutes, and with far greater enthusiasm than a demand ever produced.

Friendliness does not require interrogation. The unspoken rule of good conversation is to let people decide which parts of their story to offer first, and a society confident in its sense of neighbourhood and nationhood can afford that patience.

1.title: Welcome to a school of newcomers
1.brief: You have been asked to give the welcome speech at the opening of the school year at an international school whose students come from more than forty countries. Write the speech, in which you reflect on what it means to belong to a community made up of newcomers.
1.briefEs: Escribe el discurso de bienvenida de un colegio internacional reflexionando sobre qué significa pertenecer a una comunidad de recién llegados.
criteria: Direct address to the audience, a clear opening and a memorable closing line.
Perfect and continuous aspect for nuance (has been pretending, I had not expected).
At least one stative verb used dynamically (I am being entirely honest).
Word formation with un-, -ness or -hood, and an idiom of belonging (to find your feet, to put down roots).
1.model:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome.

Some of you arrived last night, still carrying the suitcase and the strange silence of a journey that has not quite ended. Others have been here for years and have watched this ceremony from the back row. I would like to speak to all of you, but especially to those who are wondering, right now, whether you will ever feel at home.

I had not expected to feel so nervous this morning, and I am being entirely honest when I say it reminds me of my own first day here nine years ago. I was convinced that everybody else had already found their feet. They had not. I learned that nearly everyone in this hall has been pretending, at one time or another, to be more settled than they were.

Belonging, you see, is not a certificate handed over on the first day. It is built, slowly, from small acts: lending a pen, saying a name correctly, sitting beside someone who is sitting alone. A community of newcomers has one great advantage. Nobody here owns the right way of doing things, and so everyone is free to help decide it.

Today you are being asked to do something difficult and a little unfashionable. You are being asked to be curious about people who are unlike you, to tolerate misunderstanding and to remain generous when your patience runs short. Friendship across languages takes extra effort, and a good deal of kindness. It is worth every minute of it.

In a few years, many of you will leave and put down roots elsewhere. Wherever you go, you will take with you the memory of a place where neighbourhood meant the whole world. So let me finish with a simple wish: that each of you find, before the end of this term, one person who is glad you came.

Welcome home.

2.title: Who should police online speech?
2.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — A duty to intervene
Social media companies can no longer claim to be neutral pipes through which information simply flows. Their algorithms decide what billions of people see, and those algorithms reward outrage and falsehood because they keep users engaged. Having profited from the spread of misinformation, the platforms have a clear responsibility to limit it, by labelling misleading content, slowing its circulation and removing material that causes demonstrable harm.

Text 2 — The danger of the referee
Handing private companies the power to decide what is true is a cure that may prove worse than the disease. Moderators make mistakes, and their errors fall disproportionately on unpopular minorities and dissenting voices. Yesterday's 'misinformation' has, on more than one occasion, become today's accepted view. Rather than censorship, we need citizens equipped to judge for themselves and a public sphere in which bad arguments are defeated by better ones.
2.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre quién debe controlar los contenidos en redes sociales.
criteria: Both texts summarised in your own words, with reporting verbs of nuance (concede, allege, insinuate, maintain).
At least one it-cleft and one wh-cleft for emphasis.
Inversion after a negative or restrictive adverbial (Not only…, Rarely…, Only when…).
A clear personal evaluation that goes beyond the texts.
2.model:
The two texts examine whether social media platforms should take responsibility for limiting misinformation, and they arrive at opposing conclusions.

The first writer maintains that platforms are far from passive channels. Because their algorithms promote whatever keeps users engaged, and falsehood tends to do exactly that, the companies have benefited from the problem and should therefore act against it, flagging dubious claims, reducing their reach and deleting genuinely harmful material. What makes this argument compelling is its focus on design: it is the systems, not merely the users, that deserve scrutiny.

The second writer, by contrast, warns that entrusting corporations with the role of arbiter of truth is dangerous. Moderation is fallible, she argues, and its mistakes tend to silence those who are already marginalised. She also points out that ideas once dismissed as false have sometimes been vindicated. Her alternative is a better-informed public capable of rejecting weak arguments on its own.

Not only are both positions defensible, but each identifies a weakness in the other. The second writer is right that removal is a blunt instrument, yet she rather underestimates how difficult it is for individuals to judge claims that are engineered to bypass their scepticism. The first writer, meanwhile, concedes too little to the risk of error.

In my view, it is the algorithms rather than individual posts that should be the primary target of regulation. Only when platforms are required to stop rewarding outrage will the volume of misinformation fall, and this approach would leave far fewer decisions about truth in the hands of moderators. Education, as the second writer insists, remains essential, but it works best in an environment that is not rigged against it.

2.title: Advertising that crosses the line
2.brief: A national newspaper recently published an article praising a new advertising campaign for an energy drink aimed at teenagers, which uses the slogan 'Sleep is for the weak'. Write a letter to the editor responding to the article, explaining why you consider the campaign irresponsible and what action you believe should be taken.
2.briefEs: Escribe una carta al director de un periódico criticando una campaña publicitaria dirigida a adolescentes y proponiendo medidas.
criteria: Appropriate formal letter conventions and a clear reason for writing.
Fronting and inversion for emphasis (Seldom have I…, So persuasive is the slogan that…).
Reporting verbs with nuance to represent the article fairly (the writer concedes / insinuates / claims).
A controlled shift of register: rhetorical force without losing formality.
2.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing in response to your article of 14 March, in which the new advertising campaign for an energy drink was described as 'bold, witty and refreshingly honest'. Seldom have I read a piece that so completely overlooked the responsibilities that come with addressing a young audience.

Your correspondent concedes that the slogan 'Sleep is for the weak' is provocative, but insinuates that only humourless adults could object to it. I would suggest that the objection has nothing to do with humour. What concerns me, as a parent and a secondary school teacher, is that the campaign presents sleep deprivation, a well-documented risk to adolescent health, as a badge of strength. So effective is the message that several of my students have already adopted the phrase, usually while explaining why they have not done their homework.

It is worth recalling what the evidence tells us. Teenagers need considerably more sleep than adults, and chronic tiredness has been linked to poor concentration, low mood and an increased likelihood of accidents. A product that combines high levels of caffeine with a message ridiculing rest is not merely tasteless; it actively undermines the efforts of schools and families to promote healthier habits.

Nor is this simply a matter of personal taste. Advertising standards rightly prohibit campaigns that encourage behaviour likely to harm the health of children. I would therefore urge the relevant authority to review the campaign without delay, and I would invite the manufacturer to consider whether a short-term boost in sales is worth the damage to its reputation.

Your article praised the campaign for its honesty. The honest truth, however, is that sleep is not for the weak. It is for anyone who wishes to think clearly, and teenagers deserve to be told so.

Yours faithfully,

Elena Ruiz

2.title: In defence of the public library
2.brief: Your town council intends to close the central library and replace it with a car park. You have been invited to speak at the public meeting. Write the speech you would deliver, aiming to persuade councillors and residents to reconsider.
2.briefEs: Escribe el discurso que pronunciarías en una reunión pública para convencer al ayuntamiento de que no cierre la biblioteca central.
criteria: At least two it-clefts or wh-clefts used to emphasise key points.
At least two inversions after a negative or restrictive adverbial (Never before…, Only when…, Not once…).
A rule of three, a rhetorical question and a memorable closing line.
A formal address to the audience and a clear call to action.
2.model:
Madam Chair, councillors, neighbours,

Thank you for allowing me to speak. I want to begin with a question that nobody on the committee has yet asked: what exactly are we proposing to remove?

The answer, according to the report, is a building that costs too much to heat. But it is not the building that matters. What the library provides is a place where a child without a quiet room can do her homework, where a pensioner can learn to send an email, and where a jobseeker can print a CV without paying for the privilege. Warmth, quiet and a little dignity: that is what would disappear.

It is the people who cannot afford alternatives who will suffer most. Never before has the cost of home internet been so high, and rarely has the need for free access been so plain. Only when a library has closed do communities discover how much work it was quietly doing, and by then the damage cannot easily be undone.

The report argues that digital services will fill the gap. I would ask the committee to consider how many of its own members have recently tried to renew a passport online without help. Digital inclusion, it seems, is something one can legislate for without ever meeting those excluded. Not once does the document mention the thousand people who visit each week, nor the forty volunteers who run its reading groups for nothing.

Councillors, no one is asking you to ignore the budget. What I am asking is that you look again, and that you consult the people who use the building before you lock its doors. Pause the vote. Hold a proper consultation. Then decide.

A town that closes its library has not saved money; it has simply chosen to stop investing in its own future. Let us not be that town.

2.title: Sorry, not sorry: the anatomy of the non-apology
2.brief: A journal of rhetoric has invited critical essays on public language. Write a critical essay analysing the 'non-apology' (for example, 'mistakes were made' or 'I'm sorry if anyone was offended') as a rhetorical strategy: how it works, why speakers choose it and whether audiences should accept it.
2.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo crítico sobre la 'no disculpa' como estrategia retórica: cómo funciona, por qué se usa y si el público debería aceptarla.
criteria: At least one it-cleft and one wh-cleft used for emphasis.
At least two inversions after a negative or restrictive adverbial (Not only…, Seldom…, Under no circumstances…).
Fronting for focus (Particularly telling is…, Equally damaging is…).
A clear thesis, a critical stance and a balanced conclusion that avoids sweeping claims.
2.model:
Sorry, Not Sorry: The Anatomy of the Non-Apology

An apology is meant to do three things: acknowledge a wrong, accept responsibility and promise to do better. The non-apology performs the gesture while quietly removing each of these. 'Mistakes were made' is the classic example, a sentence in which the errors exist but nobody commits them. This essay argues that such statements are not clumsy attempts at contrition but carefully designed instruments, and that audiences are entitled to treat them with scepticism.

Consider how they work. The passive voice deletes the agent; the conditional, as in 'if anyone was offended', transfers the problem to the listener's sensitivity. Particularly telling is the choice of verb: people are 'disappointed', 'concerned' or 'saddened', never guilty. What these formulations achieve is a posture of regret without the cost of admission, and it is precisely this gap that makes them useful to people with something to lose.

Why do speakers choose them? Not only do lawyers advise against admissions of liability, but public figures also fear that a full apology will be read as weakness. Seldom does a spokesperson speak for himself, and the safest sentence is the one that can be quoted without consequence. It is the institution, rather than the individual, that is being protected.

Yet the strategy carries a risk. Under no circumstances can trust be rebuilt by language that audiences recognise as evasive. Equally damaging is the cynicism that spreads when apologies are known to be empty: people begin to expect nothing from them, and so even genuine regret is met with suspicion.

Should we, then, reject every qualified apology? Not necessarily. Some situations are genuinely complex, and a hedged statement may reflect honest uncertainty rather than evasion. What matters is whether the speaker names the harm, accepts a share of the blame and proposes a remedy. Where all three are missing, we are right to conclude that what we have heard is a performance.

2.title: Keep the debating society
2.brief: The head teacher of your school has announced that the debating society will be closed next term to save time for exam preparation. Write a formal persuasive letter to the head teacher urging a reversal, presenting your arguments and suggesting a compromise.
2.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal persuasiva a la directora para que no cierre el club de debate, con argumentos y una propuesta de compromiso.
criteria: Formal letter conventions and a clear statement of purpose.
Fronting or inversion for emphasis (So valuable was…, Rarely have I…, Only through… can…).
At least one it-cleft and one wh-cleft.
A courteous but firm tone, with a concrete compromise proposed.
2.model:
Dear Mrs Whitaker,

I am writing to urge you to reconsider the decision, announced on Monday, to close the debating society at the end of this term. I do so as a final-year student, and as someone who has been a member for four years.

I understand that examinations must take priority, and I do not dispute that. What concerns me is the assumption that debating competes with academic success rather than contributing to it. Rarely have I encountered an activity that trains so many of the skills our teachers ask for: structuring an argument, selecting evidence, listening carefully and responding under pressure. Only through regular practice can such habits become automatic. Not only does it build confidence, but it also teaches students to disagree courteously, a skill in short supply in public life.

It is also worth considering who will lose most. Many of our members are quiet students who found their voices in that classroom on Thursday afternoons. So valuable was the society to one friend of mine, who was close to leaving the school last year, that she describes it as the reason she stayed. Their results have not suffered either; two of last year's finalists gained places at their first-choice universities. It is students like her, rather than the confident minority, who will be left without an alternative.

I would therefore like to propose a compromise. The society could meet fortnightly rather than weekly, during lunchtime, so that no lessons or revision periods are affected. Members could also be asked to run short sessions in which younger pupils practise oral presentations for their English assessments. In this way, the club would demonstrably support the school's priorities, not distract from them.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss these ideas with you, and I am confident that other members would be glad to join me. Thank you for considering this request.

Yours sincerely,

Marta Gómez

2.title: Thirty seconds to persuade
2.brief: A broadsheet is running a series on the state of public debate. Write an opinion article on whether short, quotable statements are damaging political discussion. Take a clear position, illustrate it with examples from public life, and acknowledge a counter-argument.
2.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de opinión sobre si las frases cortas y citables (soundbites) dañan el debate político, con una postura clara y una objeción reconocida.
criteria: A vivid opening and a clear position stated early.
At least one it-cleft, one wh-cleft and one example of fronting (Equally worrying is…).
At least two inversions after a negative or restrictive adverbial (Little did…, Not until…, Only when…).
A counter-argument conceded (admittedly) and then answered.
2.model:
Thirty Seconds to Persuade

A prime minister, we are told, has precisely eleven seconds to win over a voter in a television interview. The rest of the answer is irrelevant, since it will be cut. Whether we like it or not, this is the environment in which political argument now takes place, and I want to suggest that it is making us collectively worse at thinking.

Admittedly, the soundbite is not new. Churchill's phrases were designed to be quoted, and it would be absurd to pretend that brevity has no place in persuasion. A well-turned sentence can crystallise an idea that pages of policy could not. But what has changed is the proportion. Where the slogan was once the summary of an argument, it is now very often the whole of it.

Consider the consequences. Little did the designers of social media platforms realise that rewarding the shortest, sharpest statements would train politicians to stop developing their ideas. It is not the clever phrase itself that does the damage but the absence of anything behind it. Equally worrying is the effect on voters: those accustomed to slogans lose patience with qualification, and the honest speaker who says 'it depends' sounds weak beside the one who says 'it's obvious'.

Not until we demand longer answers will politicians have a reason to give them. Only when interviewers refuse to interrupt, and audiences reward the speaker who admits complexity, will the incentive begin to shift. What we need is not the abolition of the slogan but its demotion from conclusion to introduction.

Some will object that nobody has time for long speeches. I doubt it; millions of people will happily follow a three-hour podcast or a ten-episode drama. The problem is not our attention span but what we are given to attend to. Give us an argument, and we might surprise you.

3.title: Review: a book about the mind
3.brief: A popular science website is publishing reviews of books that change the way readers think about the mind. Write a review of a book you have read about memory, perception or decision-making. Explain what the book argues, evaluate how convincingly it does so, and say who would benefit most from reading it.
3.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de un libro de divulgación sobre la memoria, la percepción o la toma de decisiones para una web de ciencia.
criteria: Modals of speculation and deduction in present and past (must have, can't have, may well be).
A contrast between needn't have and didn't need to, or a modal perfect of criticism (should have, could have).
Will/would for assumption or characteristic behaviour (Readers will recognise…, She would always…).
Precise cognition vocabulary (discern, perceive, glimpse, bias) and a clear recommendation.
3.model:
The Unreliable Narrator Inside Your Head

Anyone who has ever argued with a sibling about a shared childhood memory will recognise the premise of 'The Editing Room', a lively and occasionally unsettling account of how the brain rewrites the past. Its author, a cognitive psychologist, argues that memory is less an archive than a newsroom, constantly revising its stories to fit what we now believe.

The early chapters are the strongest. Drawing on experiments in which volunteers were persuaded to 'remember' events that never happened, the author shows how readily we fill gaps with plausible detail. Most readers will have assumed that a vivid memory must be an accurate one; by the end of chapter three, they will be far less sure. Particularly memorable is a section on eyewitness testimony, in which she traces how a single leading question can reshape what a witness believes she perceived.

The book is less convincing when it turns to self-help. A chapter promising techniques to 'bias-proof' your decisions feels like an afterthought, and its advice, to slow down and consider alternatives, is sensible but hardly revelatory. The author needn't have included it at all; the science is fascinating enough without the promise of practical benefits. Similarly, she might have acknowledged more openly that some of the studies she cites have not been fully replicated, a caveat a careful reader can only glimpse in the endnotes.

These reservations aside, the writing is clear, witty and refreshingly free of jargon. The author has a gift for the telling example, and she will often pause mid-argument to describe an experiment so vividly that you can almost see the puzzled volunteers.

Who should read it? Students of psychology will find little that is new, but anyone curious about why their memories feel so certain, and are so often wrong, could hardly find a better introduction. It may well change the way you tell your own stories.

3.title: Trusting your gut
3.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — The wisdom of intuition
Experienced professionals often make excellent decisions in seconds, without being able to explain how. A veteran firefighter senses that a floor is about to collapse; a nurse notices that a patient 'just doesn't look right' hours before the monitors confirm it. Such intuitions are not mystical. They are the product of thousands of hours of pattern recognition, and to dismiss them in favour of slow, explicit analysis is to throw away valuable expertise.

Text 2 — The limits of the gut
Intuition feels reliable precisely because it arrives with a sense of certainty, but that certainty is often misplaced. In fields where feedback is slow or unclear, such as investment or long-term forecasting, experts' instincts perform little better than chance. Worse, gut feelings are shaped by prejudice and recent experience as much as by expertise. Important decisions should be tested against evidence, however confident we feel.
3.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre la intuición frente al análisis en la toma de decisiones.
criteria: Accurate summaries of both texts in your own words.
Modals of deduction and speculation used to evaluate claims (may well be, cannot always be).
Vocabulary of cognition and bias (perceive, discern, misplaced confidence, cognitive bias).
A balanced conclusion that identifies when each approach is appropriate.
3.model:
Both texts consider how far we should rely on intuition when making decisions, though they place their emphasis very differently.

The first text defends intuition as a form of compressed expertise. Its writer argues that skilled practitioners can discern danger or illness almost instantly because years of experience have trained them to recognise patterns they cannot consciously articulate. To disregard such judgements in favour of laborious analysis, she suggests, would be to waste knowledge that has been hard won. The examples of the firefighter and the nurse are persuasive, and most of us will have encountered professionals whose instincts proved uncannily accurate.

The second text, however, cautions that the confidence intuition brings is not proof of its accuracy. Its author observes that in areas where outcomes emerge slowly, experts' hunches may be barely more reliable than guesses, and that instinct is easily distorted by bias and by whatever happens to be fresh in our minds. Decisions of consequence, he concludes, ought to be checked against evidence.

On reflection, the two positions can be reconciled. Intuition is likely to be trustworthy only where people have had extensive practice and rapid, clear feedback, which is precisely the situation of the firefighter and the nurse. Where feedback is delayed or ambiguous, the gut may well be little more than a confident storyteller. The real skill, then, lies in recognising which kind of situation one is in. A doctor who acts on a hunch in an emergency is behaving sensibly; a minister who stakes a national budget on one cannot be said to be doing the same. Instinct deserves respect, but it should not be allowed to escape scrutiny.

3.title: The kitchen I can still smell
3.brief: A magazine invites readers to write about a memory and what it makes them wonder about their own recollection. Write a reflective essay about a childhood place or event, using it to consider how reliable your memory really is.
3.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo reflexivo sobre un lugar o suceso de tu infancia y lo que revela sobre la fiabilidad de la memoria.
criteria: Modals of speculation and deduction in present and past (must have been, can't have been, may well be).
Would for past habit and used to, with a clear difference in use.
A contrast between needn't have and didn't need to, and a modal perfect of regret (should have).
Precise cognition vocabulary (vivid, recollect, distorted) and a thoughtful conclusion.
3.model:
The Kitchen I Can Still Smell

My grandmother's kitchen in Popayán used to be, in my memory, enormous. Every Sunday we would crowd around a table that I remember as the length of a bus, while she stirred a pot the size of a bath. When I returned there last year, I discovered that the room was barely three metres wide. I can't have been such a small child that everything looked huge; I was ten when we last visited. Yet the table must have seemed vast to me, because it was where the whole family met.

That discovery set me wondering about everything else I believed I could recollect. I have a vivid picture of the day my brother fell from the mango tree, complete with the colour of his shirt and the sound of my mother shouting. My brother, however, insists that he wore blue and that my mother was at the market. One of us must be wrong, and it may well be both of us. Psychologists tell us that each time we recall an event we rebuild it, so the memory is perhaps less a photograph than a copy of a copy.

There are things I should have asked my grandmother while I could. I needn't have waited until the funeral to find out how she made that soup; she would have been delighted to tell me, and she would always answer questions about her past with more detail than anyone expected. At the time I didn't need to write anything down, or so I thought. It never occurred to me that the knowledge could vanish.

And yet the smell of cumin and burnt sugar can bring the room back at once, distorted but unmistakably hers. I have stopped worrying about whether the table was really that long. It must have been exactly as long as it felt, for the child who sat at it, and that, perhaps, is the only kind of accuracy that matters when we remember the people we love.

3.title: Review: a crime novel in which nobody can be trusted
3.brief: A newspaper's books page invites reviews of crime fiction or psychological thrillers. Write a review of a novel, real or imagined, in which the reader is left unsure whom to trust. Explain how the author builds doubt, evaluate whether it succeeds, and say who would enjoy it.
3.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de una novela de misterio, real o imaginada, en la que el lector no sabe en quién confiar: cómo genera la duda, si lo logra y a quién se la recomiendas.
criteria: Modals of deduction and speculation in present and past (must have had, can't have been, may well suspect).
A modal perfect of criticism (could have been cut, might have been sharper) and a needn't have contrast.
Will/would for assumption or characteristic behaviour (readers will assume…, she would never lie…).
Precise vocabulary of perception and suspicion (glimpse, discern, misdirection, misled) and a clear recommendation.
3.model:
Nobody Is Telling the Whole Truth

Few crime novels make the reader feel quite so foolish as 'The Quiet Tenant'. By the end of the first chapter you will have decided who the culprit is; by the end of the third, you will have changed your mind twice; and by the final page, you may well suspect that you were never meant to be sure. The setting is a coastal boarding house where a retired actor is found dead in his locked room. Everyone must have had a reason to dislike him, and nobody can have been near enough to do it, or so the guests insist.

The author's great skill is misdirection. The narrator, a young widow who runs the house, always sounds so reasonable that readers will assume she is telling the truth. She would never lie to us outright; she simply omits. A glimpse of a muddy boot here, a half-heard argument there: by the time we discern the pattern, we see that the clues must have been staring us in the face all along. It is a clever trick, and it is performed with real confidence.

The book is not flawless. The subplot about the missing letters could have been cut without loss, and a long flashback in the middle needn't have been so detailed to make its point. The prose, moreover, sometimes mistakes atmosphere for substance: there are only so many foggy mornings a reader can tolerate. Some of the dialogue might have been sharper had the author trusted her characters to be less polite.

Yet these are quibbles. The final twist, which I will not spoil, is earned rather than imposed, and it rewards a second reading. Admirers of traditional detective stories will relish the closed-circle setup, while readers who prefer modern psychological thrillers will find enough unease to keep them turning pages. If you enjoy being misled by an expert, this is the best invitation you will receive this year.

3.title: Why you can't do two things at once
3.brief: A popular psychology magazine is running a series on beliefs about the mind that deserve to be challenged. Write an opinion article arguing that multitasking is largely a myth, drawing on everyday examples and suggesting what we should do instead.
3.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de opinión que sostenga que la multitarea es en gran parte un mito, con ejemplos cotidianos y una recomendación práctica.
criteria: Modals of speculation and deduction (must be happening, cannot be, may well be).
Will/would for typical behaviour or assumption (he will answer…, they would be astonished…).
A modal perfect of criticism (ought to have realised) and a needn't contrast.
Cognition vocabulary (attention, concentration, perceive) and a practical recommendation.
3.model:
Why You Can't Do Two Things at Once

Somewhere in the average office there is a person who will tell you, with real pride, that he is a gifted multitasker. He will answer an email while listening to a colleague and drafting a report, and he will always seem busy. What he cannot be is efficient. The evidence suggests that what we call multitasking is really rapid switching, and that each switch costs us something.

Consider what must be happening in the brain. Attention is not a tap that can be divided between two glasses; it is closer to a spotlight that jumps between objects. Every jump forces us to reload the task we left behind, which is why a message that takes a minute to read may cost five minutes of concentration. This cannot be a trivial effect: studies of drivers using phones suggest that their reaction times may well be as slow as those of people who have been drinking.

The cruel irony is that the worst multitaskers are often those who believe themselves best at it. They perceive themselves as productive because they are constantly busy, and they would be astonished to learn how many errors they miss. Many of us ought to have realised this years ago, when we first found ourselves re-reading the same paragraph for the third time while a notification pinged.

None of this means that we should abandon every habit of combining activities. You needn't give up music while you tidy the house, for nothing requires your full attention there. The difficulty arises with tasks that demand thought. For those, the advice is old-fashioned but sound: close the other tabs, silence your phone and finish one thing before beginning the next. You will probably find that the work not only improves but takes less time than you feared, and that your day feels shorter, rather than longer, for it.

3.title: Seeing is believing? Illusions and the limits of perception
3.brief: A philosophy and science journal invites critical essays on perception. Write a critical essay on what optical illusions reveal about the reliability of perception, and whether they show that we cannot trust our senses.
3.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo crítico sobre lo que revelan las ilusiones ópticas acerca de la fiabilidad de la percepción.
criteria: Modals of deduction and speculation in present and past (must reflect, may well be wrong, could not have kept…).
Will/would for typical behaviour (they will insist…, it would be impossible…).
At least one modal perfect of criticism (should have asked).
Precise cognition vocabulary (perceive, discern, bias, glimpse, deceive) and a reasoned conclusion that avoids overstatement.
3.model:
Seeing Is Believing? Illusions and the Limits of Perception

Show someone two identical horizontal lines, one flanked by arrowheads pointing outwards and the other by arrowheads pointing in, and they will insist that the lines differ in length. Even after measuring them with a ruler, they will go on perceiving the difference. The Müller-Lyer illusion is therefore often treated as proof that our senses deceive us. This essay argues that such a conclusion goes too far.

The first thing to note is that illusions are not random errors. They are systematic, which suggests that they must reflect the way the visual system solves problems. The brain receives incomplete, ambiguous signals and must infer what is out there; it would be impossible to process every detail afresh. When it meets a pattern that resembles a corner, it assumes depth, and in the laboratory that assumption may well be wrong. In the street, it is usually right. An illusion, in other words, is a rule applied in the wrong place.

It would be a mistake, then, to say that perception is unreliable. Viewers who are fooled in a laboratory needn't be fooled in real life, where context supplies what the drawing removes. Philosophers who infer from these experiments that we can never trust our eyes should have asked how we manage to catch a ball or cross a road. A system that was truly deceptive could not have kept our ancestors alive.

Nevertheless, illusions retain real value. They remind us that perception is an interpretation, not a recording, and that confidence in what we see is no guarantee of accuracy. The same biases that make us misjudge a line may help to explain why two witnesses will glimpse the same event and discern different details. The sensible conclusion is not that we should distrust our senses, but that we should be aware of how they work, and sceptical of the feeling of certainty they produce.

4.title: Report on a graduate mentoring scheme
4.brief: Your organisation introduced a pilot mentoring scheme last year, pairing new graduate employees with senior staff. The director has asked you to write a report evaluating the scheme. Your report should assess what has worked well, identify any problems, and make recommendations about whether and how the scheme should be extended.
4.briefEs: Escribe un informe para la dirección evaluando un programa piloto de mentoría para empleados recién graduados y con recomendaciones.
criteria: Clear report layout with headings and an objective, impersonal tone.
Nominalisation and complex noun phrases (the introduction of, a reduction in staff turnover).
Participle and reduced relative clauses (staff taking part, the problems identified).
Verb patterns with a change of meaning (stopped attending / stopped to reflect; tried to arrange / tried meeting).
4.model:
Introduction
The purpose of this report is to evaluate the graduate mentoring pilot introduced in January and to make recommendations regarding its future. The findings are based on a survey completed by all twenty-four participants and on interviews with six mentors.

Strengths of the scheme
The most significant outcome has been a marked improvement in graduate retention. Of the twelve graduates taking part, eleven remain with the company, compared with an average of seven in previous intakes. Participants consistently attributed their decision to stay to the guidance received from their mentors, particularly in the early months. A number also reported a greater understanding of how decisions are made across departments, something rarely acquired through formal training alone.

Problems identified
The principal difficulty concerned time. Several mentors, faced with heavy workloads, stopped attending scheduled meetings after the first quarter, leaving their mentees uncertain whom to approach. Others tried to arrange sessions outside working hours, which proved unpopular. In addition, the absence of clear objectives meant that some pairings drifted into informal conversations with little lasting value. Mentors who tried setting specific goals at the outset, by contrast, described their sessions as considerably more productive.

Recommendations
In view of these findings, it is recommended that the scheme be extended to all graduate employees from next year, subject to the following changes:
• the allocation of protected time, of at least two hours per month, for mentoring activities;
• the introduction of a brief training session for mentors, covering goal-setting and feedback;
• a mid-year review allowing either party to request a different pairing if the relationship is not working.

Conclusion
Despite the problems outlined above, the pilot has demonstrated clear benefits at relatively low cost. With the adjustments proposed, there is every reason to believe that an extended scheme would make a lasting contribution to the development and retention of new staff.

4.title: Is failure overrated?
4.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — Fail fast, fail often
The most innovative organisations treat failure not as a disgrace but as information. Every unsuccessful experiment eliminates a possibility and brings the team closer to a solution. Cultures that punish mistakes produce employees who never take risks, and companies that never take risks are eventually overtaken by those that do. Celebrating intelligent failure is therefore not a luxury but a condition of progress.

Text 2 — The cult of the comeback
It has become fashionable to romanticise failure, particularly among those who have already succeeded. The entrepreneur who jokes about his three bankrupt start-ups rarely mentions the family money that cushioned each fall. For most people, failure means debt, anxiety and lost opportunities that never return. Encouraging the young to 'fail often' without acknowledging these costs is not inspiring; it is irresponsible.
4.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre si se idealiza el fracaso.
criteria: Faithful summaries of both texts without lifting phrases.
Nominalisation for a formal academic style (the celebration of failure, a reluctance to take risks).
Participle clauses to condense information (Having summarised…, Writing from…).
Collocations with make/take/do/have at C2 (take a calculated risk, make allowances for, have a bearing on).
4.model:
Both texts examine the current enthusiasm for failure as a route to success, but they assess its value in sharply contrasting ways.

The first text presents failure as a source of learning. According to its writer, each unsuccessful attempt narrows the range of possibilities and thereby advances the search for a solution. Organisations that penalise error, he argues, discourage risk-taking and will ultimately lose ground to more adventurous competitors. The celebration of well-judged failure is consequently portrayed as essential to innovation. This is a reasonable position, and it has a clear bearing on fields such as research and product design, where experimentation is unavoidable.

The second text, however, questions who can actually afford to fail. Its author suggests that the glorification of failure is largely the work of people whose setbacks were softened by wealth or connections, and that for the majority the consequences are far more serious and lasting. Urging young people to embrace failure without recognising these risks is, in her view, reckless. Writing from the perspective of those without such safety nets, she raises a point that the first text conspicuously ignores.

In my opinion, the two positions are complementary rather than contradictory. The first describes the conditions under which failure can be productive; the second reminds us that those conditions are unevenly distributed. The real challenge, therefore, is not to choose between celebrating and fearing failure, but to extend to more people the security that makes it possible to take a calculated risk. Institutions that genuinely wish to encourage innovation must make allowances for mistakes, but they must also ensure that a single failure does not have ruinous consequences for those who make it.

4.title: Executive report: four-day week pilot
4.brief: Your company's board is considering a permanent four-day working week following a six-month pilot in two departments. Write an executive report for the board summarising the results, weighing the benefits against the risks, and making a clear recommendation.
4.briefEs: Escribe un informe ejecutivo para la junta sobre un piloto de semana laboral de cuatro días: resultados, riesgos y una recomendación clara.
criteria: Report layout with brief headings (Summary, Findings, Risks, Recommendation) and an impersonal tone.
Nominalisation and complex noun phrases (a reduction in absenteeism, the introduction of the new rota).
Participle and reduced relative clauses (staff taking part, the gains observed).
At least two verb patterns with a change of meaning (stopped checking, tried to cover / tried reorganising, remember to log) and one collocation with take/make (take a calculated risk).
4.model:
Executive Report: Four-Day Week Pilot

Summary
This report evaluates the six-month pilot of a four-day working week in the Customer Service and Finance departments and recommends a course of action. The conclusions are based on survey data from sixty-two participants and on performance figures supplied by both departments. In brief, the pilot has delivered a clear improvement in staff wellbeing without a significant loss of output, though a number of risks require management.

Findings
The most notable result was a reduction in absenteeism of 18 per cent among staff taking part, accompanied by a marked rise in reported job satisfaction. Output, measured by cases resolved and invoices processed, remained broadly stable. Several employees reported that they stopped checking email on their day off, which they identified as the main reason for returning refreshed. Customer satisfaction scores, by contrast, fell slightly during the first month before recovering, which suggests that the early disruption was temporary rather than structural. Managers, however, noted that the introduction of the new rota made it harder to schedule meetings, and clients contacting the company on Fridays experienced longer waiting times.

Risks
Two risks deserve attention. First, the gains observed may not be reproduced in departments where work is driven by external deadlines. Second, there is a danger that staff will feel pressure to compress five days of work into four, which would defeat the purpose. Teams which tried to cover Fridays by extending daily hours reported higher fatigue than those that tried reorganising their tasks.

Recommendation
It is recommended that the board take a calculated risk and extend the scheme for a further twelve months, subject to three conditions:
• the provision of cover on Fridays through a reduced rota;
• the monitoring of workloads, with staff encouraged to remember to log overtime;
• a formal review in the final quarter, drawing on customer satisfaction data.
Should the results hold, a permanent adoption could be considered at that point.

4.title: Requesting a grant for postgraduate study
4.brief: You are a final-year engineering student who has been offered a place on a postgraduate programme abroad but cannot afford the fees. Write a formal persuasive letter to a charitable foundation that funds young professionals, asking for a grant. Explain your achievements, your plans and the benefit to your community.
4.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal persuasiva a una fundación solicitando una beca para un posgrado en el extranjero: logros, planes y beneficio para tu comunidad.
criteria: Formal letter conventions and a clear request.
Nominalisation and complex noun phrases (my acceptance onto the programme, an improvement in water quality).
Participle and reduced relative clauses (a project funded by…, students working in…).
At least two verb patterns with a change of meaning (regret to say, remember visiting, tried to negotiate / tried borrowing) and one collocation with make/take (take the initiative).
4.model:
Dear Members of the Selection Panel,

I am writing to apply for the Hernández Foundation Grant for Young Professionals, which I hope will make it possible for me to accept a place on the Master's programme in Water Engineering at the University of Delft.

My acceptance onto the programme was the culmination of five years of study, but it has been accompanied by a difficulty I cannot overcome alone: the tuition fees, which exceed my family's annual income. I do not make this request lightly, and I regret to say that I have exhausted every alternative: I tried to negotiate a deferral with the university, tried borrowing from relatives and applied to a scholarship programme that closed before my results arrived.

I would like to draw the panel's attention to my record of practical contribution. During my degree I took the initiative in establishing a student group working in rural communities around Boyacá, where we designed low-cost filtration units for six schools. The project, funded by a small university grant, produced a measurable improvement in water quality, and I remember visiting one school to find the children drinking from a tap for the first time. I have never forgotten that afternoon, and I have never stopped trying to make something of it.

The programme in Delft would equip me to extend this work. I plan to return after graduating and to establish a regional centre for water treatment, offering training to technicians and advising municipalities facing contamination problems. The expected benefit is considerable: an estimated forty communities could be reached within five years. Unlike many applicants, I am not seeking to leave the country permanently, and I am willing to sign an agreement to that effect.

I should be glad to provide references, transcripts and a detailed budget. This grant would be an investment not only in one student but in the development of an entire region. Thank you for your time and attention.

Yours faithfully,

Camila Restrepo

4.title: What ambition really demands
4.brief: You have been invited to give the keynote speech at an awards evening for young entrepreneurs in your region. Write a speech, about five minutes long, in which you reflect on what ambition really demands and encourage the audience without resorting to clichés.
4.briefEs: Escribe el discurso principal de una gala de jóvenes emprendedores: qué exige realmente la ambición, con ánimo pero sin tópicos.
criteria: Direct address, a strong opening and a memorable close.
Nominalisation and complex noun phrases (the pursuit of achievement, a willingness to continue).
Participle and reduced relative clauses (those standing here tonight, the businesses founded in this room).

At least two verb patterns with a change of meaning (stopped trading / stopped to think, remember sitting / remember to celebrate, went on to employ / went on believing) and one collocation with make/take.
4.model:
Ladies and gentlemen, finalists, families,

When I was asked to speak tonight, I was told to be inspiring. I decided instead to be honest, which I hope you will find more useful.

Ambition, as we usually describe it, is a question of appetite. Those standing here tonight have it in abundance. But the pursuit of achievement is not sustained by appetite alone. It depends on a willingness to continue when the novelty has worn off, and on the quieter habits of preparation that nobody applauds. Ambition without patience is merely impatience wearing a better suit.

Let me tell you about my first business, a bicycle repair shop. In its first year I made every mistake available. I priced too low, I hired a friend who did not want the job, and I forgot to renew our insurance. I remember sitting in the empty workshop one evening, calculating how long we could survive. I could have stopped trading there. Instead, I stopped to think, which is a different thing, and the answer I found was not a grand strategy but a modest correction: charge more, and call every customer back within a day.

That shop went on to employ eleven people. I would like to say that I went on believing in it throughout, but belief came and went. What stayed was routine. The businesses founded in this room will face the same test: not the dramatic moment of the launch, but the long, unglamorous middle.

So let me offer three requests. Take the risks that frighten you a little, and refuse the ones that frighten you a lot. Make time for the people who tell you the truth. And remember to celebrate, because a success unmarked is a success half-lived.

Congratulations to all of you. Now, please, enjoy the evening.

4.title: Knowing when to stop
4.brief: A magazine for young professionals is publishing reflective essays under the title 'Knowing when to stop'. Write a reflective essay about a goal you abandoned or changed, what the decision cost you and what it taught you about ambition.
4.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo reflexivo sobre una meta que abandonaste o cambiaste, lo que te costó y lo que aprendiste sobre la ambición.
criteria: Nominalisation and complex noun phrases (my abandonment of the career, a growing sense of dread).
Participle and reduced relative clauses (having practised…, a dream inherited from…).
At least two verb patterns with a change of meaning (tried to ignore / tried practising, regret to say / regret choosing, stopped to ask).
At least one collocation with make/take/have (make a decision, take stock, have a bearing on).
4.model:
Knowing When to Stop

For eleven years I played the cello, and for nine of them I intended to become a professional. Having practised for several hours a day since the age of twelve, I considered the decision to enter the conservatory almost inevitable. It was a dream inherited, if I am honest, from a mother who had never had the chance herself.

The first doubts were small. I began to skip practice on days when I was tired, and then to forget that I had ever enjoyed it. At nineteen, I took stock for the first time: I could play well, but not, I realised, brilliantly, and the gap between the two was exactly the gap that mattered. I tried to ignore it. I tried practising longer, then differently, then with a new teacher. Nothing changed the underlying arithmetic.

The day I made the decision to stop was unspectacular. I remember putting the cello in its case and feeling not grief but a strange lightness. I regret to say that the conversation with my mother was harder than the decision itself, and for some months her disappointment had a bearing on how I saw myself. I stopped to ask what I wanted, and for the first time in a decade I did not know.

Today I work as a translator, and I play the cello for pleasure, without audience or ambition. I do not regret choosing differently, though I do regret not asking the question sooner. My abandonment of the career taught me something that no conservatory could have: that persistence is a virtue only when it serves a goal one still holds. A growing sense of dread should be treated as information, not weakness.

Ambition, I now believe, is less a matter of refusing to quit than of deciding, carefully and in good time, what is worth the effort.

5.title: AI in the laboratory
5.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — A new scientific revolution
Artificial intelligence is reported to have predicted the structures of millions of proteins, identified promising antibiotics and detected patterns in astronomical data that human researchers had overlooked for decades. By taking over the most laborious stages of research, AI frees scientists to concentrate on the questions that matter most. Far from threatening science, it is likely to accelerate discovery on a scale not seen since the invention of the microscope.

Text 2 — Answers without understanding
A prediction is not an explanation. When an algorithm identifies a promising compound, it rarely tells us why, and science that cannot explain its own results risks becoming a form of sophisticated guesswork. There is also a danger that research priorities will be shaped by whatever data happens to be available to train the models, rather than by the questions most worth asking.
5.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre el papel de la inteligencia artificial en la investigación científica.
criteria: Reporting passives and passive infinitives (is said to have, is thought to be, appears to have been).
Hedging and impersonal structures (it would appear, arguably, there is some evidence that).
Academic collocations (draw conclusions, pose a challenge, shed light on).
A reasoned personal view that weighs both texts.
5.model:
The two texts consider the growing role of artificial intelligence in scientific research, the first celebrating its potential and the second questioning what kind of knowledge it produces.

According to the first writer, AI has already achieved remarkable results, from modelling protein structures to uncovering overlooked patterns in data. By automating time-consuming tasks, it is said to allow researchers to focus on the most significant problems, and its impact is compared to that of the microscope. The achievements cited are undeniably impressive, and it would appear that AI can indeed shed light on problems that have resisted conventional methods for years. Nevertheless, the text arguably treats speed of discovery as if it were the only measure of scientific progress.

The second writer addresses precisely this limitation. She argues that predictions generated by algorithms frequently come without any account of the mechanisms behind them, and that a science unable to explain its findings is in danger of becoming educated guesswork. She also warns that the availability of data, rather than the importance of a question, may come to determine what is studied.

In my view, both concerns are legitimate, but they are not incompatible. AI is best regarded as a powerful instrument for generating hypotheses, which must then be tested and explained by human researchers. There is some evidence that this is already happening in many laboratories, where algorithmic predictions are treated as starting points rather than conclusions. The greater challenge, I would suggest, is institutional: funding bodies must continue to support questions that do not lend themselves to data-driven approaches. If they do so, AI need not undermine scientific understanding; it may well deepen it.

5.title: Privacy is not dead
5.brief: A technology magazine is running a series of articles titled 'Is privacy dead?'. Write an article responding to the question. You should consider how much personal data people now give away, why it matters, and what individuals and governments can realistically do to protect privacy.
5.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para una revista de tecnología respondiendo a la pregunta '¿Ha muerto la privacidad?'.
criteria: An engaging title and a lively but controlled semi-formal register.
Causatives (have your data analysed, get your settings changed, have someone check).
Reporting passives (is estimated to, is believed to have been).
Hedging language to avoid overstatement (arguably, it seems, to a large extent).
5.model:
Privacy Isn't Dead. It's Just Badly Neglected.

This morning, before I had finished my first coffee, I had my location tracked by three apps, my heart rate logged by a watch and my reading habits analysed by a news site I barely remember signing up for. None of this was dramatic. None of it required a hacker in a dark room. And that, arguably, is the problem: privacy is not being stolen from us so much as quietly given away.

The scale of that giveaway is hard to grasp. The average smartphone is estimated to share data with dozens of companies every day, most of which its owner has never heard of. Much of this information seems harmless in isolation. Combined, however, it can reveal where we live, whom we love, what we fear and how much we might be willing to pay. Several large databases are believed to have been sold on or leaked in recent years, often without the people concerned ever finding out.

Why should we care if we have nothing to hide? Because privacy is not about hiding; it is about control. It allows us to decide who knows what about us, and to change our minds. Without it, we become, to a large extent, predictable, and therefore easier to manipulate.

So what can be done? Individually, quite a lot more than most of us bother to do. It takes ten minutes to get your app permissions reviewed, and many phones will now have unnecessary tracking switched off at a single tap. But individual effort has limits. Governments must require that privacy be the default setting rather than an option buried in the menus, and they must have companies' data practices audited by regulators with real powers.

Privacy, then, is not dead. It is simply in poor health, and like most patients, it will recover only if somebody takes it seriously.

5.title: Executive report: facial recognition at stadium entrances
5.brief: A football federation is considering using facial recognition at stadium entrances to identify banned supporters. Write an executive report for its board assessing the proposal's benefits, risks and legal and ethical implications, and recommending a course of action.
5.briefEs: Escribe un informe ejecutivo para la junta de una federación sobre el uso de reconocimiento facial en estadios: beneficios, riesgos, implicaciones legales y recomendación.
criteria: Report layout with headings and an impersonal, objective tone.
At least two reporting passives (is said to, are reported to have, is believed to).
At least one causative (have the policy reviewed).
Hedging (arguably, it would appear, there is some evidence that) and academic collocations (pose a challenge, draw conclusions, shed light on).
5.model:
Executive Report: Facial Recognition at Stadium Entrances

Summary
This report considers whether the Federation should introduce facial recognition at stadium entrances to identify supporters subject to banning orders. On the evidence available, the technology offers some security benefits but poses significant challenges, and it is recommended that adoption be deferred pending an independent review.

Potential benefits
The system is said to identify banned individuals within seconds, and trials in two other leagues are reported to have reduced entry by barred supporters. There is some evidence that visible deterrence has also improved the atmosphere at matches. The Federation's own security staff, meanwhile, are understood to have welcomed the proposal, since manual checks at busy gates are slow and prone to error. It would appear, however, that these results derive from the clubs themselves, and no independent study has yet been published, so conclusions should be drawn with caution.

Risks
Accuracy poses the central challenge. Facial recognition software is believed to perform less reliably on women and on people with darker skin, which would arguably expose the Federation to claims of discrimination. Moreover, the images of thousands of law-abiding spectators would be processed, raising serious questions about consent and about how long the data is retained. Nor is it clear that the technology would be proportionate, given that breaches of banning orders are relatively rare. Fans have already been reported to be considering a legal challenge.

Recommendation
It is recommended that the Board:
• defer any purchase until the software has been independently tested for accuracy across demographic groups;
• have the proposed data-retention policy reviewed by a specialist lawyer;
• commission a consultation with supporters' groups, which may shed light on concerns not yet identified.
Should these steps be completed satisfactorily, a limited pilot at a single ground could then be considered. Until then, the cost of the system, estimated at several hundred thousand pounds, cannot be justified.

5.title: Editing the human genome: where should we draw the line?
5.brief: A bioethics journal is inviting critical essays on emerging technologies. Write a critical essay on gene editing in humans: where, if anywhere, the line between treating disease and enhancing people should be drawn, and who should decide.
5.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo crítico sobre la edición genética en humanos: dónde trazar la línea entre tratar enfermedades y mejorar personas, y quién decide.
criteria: At least two reporting passives (is widely believed to have, is said to have, are thought to have).
At least one causative or passive causative (have the research regulated, get desirable traits edited).
Hedging (arguably, it seems, to some extent, there is a possibility that) to avoid overstatement.
Academic collocations (draw a distinction, pose a dilemma, shed light on) and a reasoned conclusion.
5.model:
Editing the Human Genome: Where Should We Draw the Line?

When a Chinese scientist announced in 2018 that he had edited the genes of two babies, the reaction was swift and almost unanimous. He is widely believed to have acted prematurely, and the experiment is said to have shocked even researchers who support the technology in principle. Yet the episode did not settle the underlying question. It merely made it urgent: should we ever edit the human genome, and if so, for what?

The conventional answer draws a distinction between therapy and enhancement. Correcting a mutation that causes a fatal disease is regarded as acceptable; selecting for height, intelligence or appearance is not. The distinction is intuitive, but it is arguably less stable than it looks. Is a child's vulnerability to depression a disease or a trait? Is protection against a common virus a treatment or an upgrade? The boundary, it seems, is drawn by social convention at least as much as by biology.

This poses a dilemma for regulators. If the line is placed too conservatively, families who wish to have inherited conditions prevented in their children will be denied relief; if it is placed too liberally, there is a genuine possibility that only the wealthy will get desirable traits edited, entrenching existing inequalities. Neither outcome seems acceptable, and it would be unwise to assume that the market, left alone, will find a balance.

What the debate lacks, to some extent, is evidence. Long-term effects are poorly understood, and early experiments are thought to have caused unintended changes elsewhere in the genome. Until research has shed light on these risks, caution seems to be the only defensible position.

My conclusion is therefore modest.
