Gene editing for serious disease may well be justified once its safety is established, but decisions about what counts as serious should not be left to scientists or companies alone. Society, which will have to live with the consequences, ought to have the research regulated through open and democratic debate.

5.title: Protecting health data
5.brief: Many health and fitness apps collect sensitive information and share it with third parties. Write a formal persuasive letter to the Minister for Digital Affairs urging the government to introduce stricter rules, explaining the problem and proposing specific measures.
5.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal persuasiva a la ministra de asuntos digitales pidiendo reglas más estrictas para las apps de salud, con medidas concretas.
criteria: Formal letter conventions with a clear purpose and a courteous but firm tone.
At least two reporting passives (are estimated to, are reported to have, are believed to).
At least one causative (can have the privacy practices checked).
Hedging (arguably, it would seem) and academic collocations (raise concerns, pose a risk, draw attention to, take steps).
5.model:
Dear Minister,

I am writing to draw your attention to a matter that I believe requires urgent legislative action: the sharing of users' health data by mobile applications.

Millions of citizens now use apps to track their sleep, their menstrual cycles, their mental health and their medication. These apps are estimated to share data with an average of several dozen external companies, and a number of them are reported to have passed information to advertisers without clear consent. Users who believed they were keeping a private diary have, in effect, been providing a free supply of intimate material to the marketing industry.

The risks are not hypothetical. Insurers and employers are believed to be interested in such data, and it would seem only a matter of time before it is used to make decisions about people who have never agreed to its use. Health information is arguably the most sensitive kind we possess, and its misuse poses a risk that cannot be reversed once the information has escaped.

I would therefore urge the Government to take three steps. First, apps handling health data should be required to obtain explicit, separate consent for each category of sharing. Second, there should be an independent registry, so that citizens can have the privacy practices of any application checked before they download it. Third, penalties should be high enough to deter, because modest fines are widely seen as a cost of doing business.

I recognise that the industry will raise concerns about innovation. That is a legitimate argument, but it should not be allowed to outweigh the basic right of a patient to decide who knows about her condition. Responsible developers, moreover, have little to fear from rules which mainly affect those who profit from secrecy.

I should be grateful for the opportunity to discuss these proposals with your officials, and I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Laura Benítez

5.title: Judged by a machine
5.brief: A business magazine is asking readers whether companies should use algorithms to screen job applicants. Write an opinion article taking a clear position, with examples and a fair treatment of the opposing view.
5.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de opinión sobre si las empresas deben usar algoritmos para filtrar candidatos, con una postura clara y una objeción reconocida.
criteria: At least two reporting passives or impersonal structures (is said to, is widely reported to have, it is claimed that).
At least one causative or passive causative (have her application rejected, have their systems audited).
Hedging (arguably, tends to, to some extent) and at least two academic collocations (raise questions, pose a threat, draw conclusions).
A clear position, a counter-argument acknowledged and a firm closing line.
5.model:
Judged by a Machine

Somewhere tonight, a qualified accountant will have her application rejected before a human being has read a word of it. The software that sifted it is said to save companies thousands of hours; it is also, arguably, a quiet scandal. I want to argue that algorithmic screening of job applicants should not be used without strict human oversight.

The case in its favour is not trivial. Companies receive hundreds of applications for a single post, and recruiters, being human, are prone to fatigue and prejudice. It is claimed that software, by contrast, treats every CV in the same way. To some extent that may be true. A well-designed system could, in principle, ignore a candidate's name, age and postcode more consistently than a tired manager at the end of a long week.

The trouble is that the systems learn from the past. If a firm has historically hired mostly men, an algorithm trained on its records will tend to prefer applicants who resemble them. One large company is widely reported to have abandoned a tool for precisely this reason. Such cases raise questions about whether bias has been removed or simply automated, and made harder to challenge, since nobody can interview a formula.

What alarms me most is the lack of accountability. Candidates who get their applications rejected by software are rarely told why, and they have no means of appealing. That poses a real threat to fairness, and it is difficult to draw any other conclusion from the evidence.

Does this mean we should ban the technology? No. But employers should be required to have their systems audited by independent experts, to explain rejections in plain language and to guarantee that a person reviews borderline cases. Efficiency is a fine thing; it is not a substitute for being treated as an individual.

6.title: Objecting to a wetland development
6.brief: Your local council has approved plans to drain part of a wetland on the edge of your town to build a retail park and car park. Write a letter to the council's planning committee objecting to the decision. Explain what the wetland means to the community, what the likely consequences of the development would be, and what alternative you propose.
6.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal al comité de urbanismo oponiéndote a la desecación de un humedal para construir un centro comercial.
criteria: Formal letter conventions and a clearly stated purpose.
At least two inverted conditionals (Had the committee consulted…, Should the plans proceed…, Were the wetland to be drained…).
At least three alternatives to if (provided, but for, otherwise, supposing, were it not for).
A mixed conditional linking past decisions to present consequences, and environmental collocations (flood defences, natural habitat, irreversible damage).
6.model:
Dear Members of the Planning Committee,

I am writing to object in the strongest terms to the decision, approved on 3 June, to drain part of Millbrook Marsh for the construction of a retail park and car park.

The marsh is far more than a patch of unused land. It is home to breeding wading birds, otters and several species of dragonfly that are found nowhere else in the county, and it is used daily by walkers, schools and naturalists. Had the committee consulted local residents more widely, it would have been made aware of the strength of feeling on this matter, and we would not now be facing a decision that so many regard as short-sighted.

My greatest concern, however, is flooding. The marsh acts as a natural sponge, absorbing heavy rainfall that would otherwise flow directly into the lower town. Were it not for the marsh, the floods of 2019 would almost certainly have reached far more homes than they did. Should the development proceed, the council may find itself obliged to spend considerably more on artificial flood defences than it will ever recover from business rates. Draining the wetland would also release large quantities of stored carbon, causing irreversible damage at a time when the council has committed itself to reducing emissions.

I do not dispute that the town needs investment. I would propose, however, that the retail park be located on the former bus depot site on Station Road, which has stood empty for six years and requires no loss of natural habitat. Provided the necessary road improvements are made, this site would be equally accessible to shoppers.

Supposing the committee were willing to reconsider, I and many other residents would be glad to take part in a consultation. I urge you to do so before damage is done that no future decision can undo.

Yours faithfully,

Daniel Ospina

6.title: Should we let nature take its course?
6.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — Letting go
For centuries we have managed the countryside as if it were a garden, deciding which species belong and which do not. Rewilding asks us to step back and let natural processes such as grazing, flooding and decay shape the land once more. Where it has been tried, the results have been striking: the return of birds, insects and mammals that had vanished for generations. Had we been bolder sooner, far more would have survived.

Text 2 — A luxury for the few
Rewilding is easy to champion from a city apartment. For farming communities, it can mean the loss of livelihoods, traditions and food production, and the reintroduction of predators raises real fears for livestock. Conservation that ignores the people who live on the land is unlikely to last. Nature recovery must be pursued with rural communities, not imposed upon them.
6.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre la renaturalización (rewilding) y su impacto en las comunidades rurales.
criteria: Accurate, concise summaries of both texts.
Mixed and implied conditionals (If we had acted sooner, more species would be thriving now; Otherwise…).
At least one inverted conditional or alternative to if.
Environmental collocations and compound adjectives (far-reaching, long-term, man-made).
6.model:
Both texts discuss rewilding, the restoration of land through natural processes, but whereas the first presents it as an overdue correction, the second stresses its cost to rural communities.

The first writer argues that our long-standing habit of controlling the landscape has impoverished it, and that allowing grazing, flooding and decay to resume their natural role brings remarkable ecological benefits. Long-absent species have reappeared wherever the approach has been adopted, and he implies that, had we acted earlier, many more species would be thriving today. The evidence for these benefits is well documented, and the argument is compelling as far as biodiversity is concerned.

The second writer does not reject rewilding outright but insists that it often reflects the priorities of urban supporters rather than those who live on the land. She points to the economic and cultural losses that farmers may face and to legitimate anxieties about predators attacking livestock. Unless rural people are involved as partners, she warns, conservation projects will not endure.

In my view, the second text identifies the condition on which the success of the first depends. Rewilding is a far-reaching change in how land is used, and change of that kind can only be sustained provided it commands local support. Otherwise, it risks provoking a backlash that could set conservation back for years. There are encouraging examples of schemes in which farmers are paid to restore habitats while continuing to produce food, and these seem to offer the most promising long-term model. Were such schemes to become the norm, the apparent conflict between the two writers might largely disappear.

6.title: Woodland or wasteland?
6.brief: Your neighbourhood has the chance to turn a derelict lot into an urban woodland, but residents are divided because of cost and concerns about maintenance. Write a speech to be delivered at a community meeting urging residents to vote in favour.
6.briefEs: Escribe un discurso para una reunión vecinal que anime a votar a favor de convertir un solar abandonado en un bosque urbano.
criteria: At least two inverted conditionals (Were that land to stay…, Should the vote fail…, Had we started…).
At least two alternatives to if (provided that, unless, supposing).
A mixed conditional linking a past decision to a present result.
Environmental collocations (urban heat, natural habitat, green space) and a clear call to vote.
6.model:
Good evening, neighbours.

Thank you for coming on a night when most of us would rather be at home. I will be brief, because the question before us is simple: do we want a woodland or a wasteland?

Let me begin with the lot as it is. For fifteen years it has been a place where rubbish gathers and where children are told not to play. Were that land to stay as it is, nothing would change except the size of the weeds. In summer it would go on adding to the urban heat that makes our streets unbearable at midday, and in heavy rain it would continue to send water straight into our basements.

Now consider what a wood could do. Trees lower temperatures, absorb floodwater and offer a natural habitat to birds that have nowhere else to go. Provided that we plant native species, the woodland will need very little upkeep once it is established. Unless we act, we shall have to pay anyway, through repairs and through the slow decline of the neighbourhood.

I know the objection, and it is fair: who will pay? The council has promised the saplings, and the school has offered volunteers. Supposing the first year costs more than we expect, we shall have lost a modest sum. Should the vote fail, we shall have lost something harder to measure.

Look at the park on the hill. Had our grandparents not insisted on it, we would have no green space at all today. If they had been as cautious as we are tonight, we should be standing in a car park. Somebody had the courage to plant, and we are still sitting in the shade.

Had we started a decade ago, this wood would already be tall. We cannot recover those years, but we can decide not to waste another. Please vote yes, and let us begin in the spring.

6.title: Executive report: flood risk in Puerto Alegre
6.brief: A coastal village faces increasing flood risk. Write an executive report for the regional authority assessing the situation, evaluating three options (do nothing, build a sea wall, relocate the most exposed homes) and recommending one.
6.briefEs: Escribe un informe ejecutivo para la autoridad regional sobre el riesgo de inundación de un pueblo costero: tres opciones y una recomendación.
criteria: Report layout with headings and a precise, impersonal tone.
At least two inverted conditionals (Had the dune system been maintained…, were no action to be taken, should it fail…).
At least three alternatives to if (but for, unless, provided that, only if, in the event of, otherwise).
A mixed conditional and environmental collocations (coastal erosion, irreversible damage, sea-level rise, flood defences).
6.model:
Executive Report: Flood Risk in Puerto Alegre

Summary
This report assesses the growing flood risk to the village of Puerto Alegre and compares three options. It recommends a combined approach: a limited sea wall protecting the village centre, together with the voluntary relocation of the twelve most exposed homes.

Current situation
Coastal erosion has accelerated over the past decade, and four of the last six winters have brought flooding to the lower streets. Surveys by the municipal engineer show that the shoreline has retreated by roughly four metres since 2015. Had the dune system been maintained after 2010, the present risk would almost certainly be lower; but for the removal of vegetation during construction of the beach road, the dunes might still be intact. Sea-level rise will add to the pressure, and without intervention the problem will intensify.

Options
Option 1: take no action. This is the cheapest in the short term, but were no action to be taken, repeated flooding would impose escalating repair costs and could cause irreversible damage to the village's fresh-water supply. Unless defences are improved, insurers are likely to withdraw cover.
Option 2: build a full sea wall. This would protect the whole village, provided that adequate funding is secured. However, a wall may accelerate erosion on neighbouring beaches, and should it fail in a major storm, the consequences would be severe.
Option 3: relocate exposed homes. This is socially sensitive, but it is the only option that removes the risk entirely for those affected, and it would be acceptable to residents only if compensation were fair.

Recommendation
The Authority is advised to adopt a combined approach. A smaller wall would protect the centre, while the relocation of the twelve most exposed homes would be offered on a voluntary basis. Otherwise, the village will face the same decision in ten years, at a much higher cost. In the event of a severe storm before work begins, temporary barriers should be deployed at once.

6.title: What the river remembers
6.brief: A nature-writing journal is collecting essays about places that have changed. Write a reflective essay about a river, forest, beach or other natural place you knew as a child and how it is different now, considering what its change says about our relationship with the natural world.
6.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo reflexivo sobre un lugar natural que conociste de niño y cómo ha cambiado, y qué dice eso de nuestra relación con la naturaleza.
criteria: At least two inverted conditionals or alternatives to if (Were I to…, Had I understood…, Should the channel be removed…, provided that, but for).
A mixed conditional linking a past action to a present situation (If the municipality had consulted…, the stream would still be…).
At least one implied conditional (Otherwise…, But for…).
Environmental vocabulary and compound adjectives (fast-flowing, man-made, long-term, far-reaching).
6.model:
What the River Remembers

As a child I spent every August beside the Río Fonce, a fast-flowing stream below my aunt's farm, where I learned to swim by being pushed in. It was cold and clear and loud, and it smelled of stone. Were I to describe it now, I would have to use the past tense in a sense I did not expect: it still runs, but the river I knew has gone.

The change began with a road. A man-made channel was dug to carry rainwater away from the new houses, and within a few years the stream had become shallow and brown in summer. Nobody planned this outcome. It was the quiet, cumulative effect of a hundred reasonable decisions, none of which seemed to matter at the time. But for that channel, I suspect, the pools where we swam would still exist.

Had I understood what I was seeing, I might have said something. I was fourteen, however, and the rest of the family regarded the changes as progress. If the municipality had consulted my aunt, who knew every bend, the stream would probably still be fit for swimming today. Instead the long-term consequences were left to the people who came afterwards, which means to me.

I returned last spring. Provided that the weather stays dry, my cousin told me, the water is clean enough to paddle in; otherwise the drains overflow. We stood on the bank in silence. There were plastic bottles in the reeds, and a heron, extraordinarily, standing among them as though nothing were wrong.

Perhaps that is the lesson. Rivers are patient, and nature, given even a little room, can begin a far-reaching recovery. Should the channel be removed one day, the pools might return within a generation. It would take no more than the willingness to admit that progress, like water, can be redirected.

6.title: The true price of a weekend away
6.brief: A national newspaper's environment supplement is asking whether air travel is too cheap. Write an opinion article arguing for or against taxing short-haul flights more heavily, using clear examples and acknowledging how a policy might affect ordinary families.
6.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de opinión sobre si deben gravarse más los vuelos cortos, con ejemplos y atendiendo al efecto sobre las familias.
criteria: At least two inverted conditionals (Were fares to reflect…, Should governments fail to act…).
At least three alternatives to if (provided that, as long as, unless, supposing).
A mixed conditional (If we had priced carbon sooner, the train network would be…).
Environmental collocations (greenhouse gas, carbon footprint, tipping point) and a counter-argument acknowledged.
6.model:
The True Price of a Weekend Away

A return flight costing less than a taxi to the airport is, on the face of it, a bargain. Yet cheap flights are only cheap because somebody else pays the bill: the future residents of coastal cities, drought-hit farms and flooded towns. I want to argue that short-haul flights should be taxed more heavily, and that the fairest way to do so is to make the polluter, not the planet, pay.

The numbers are not subtle. A handful of short return flights can produce as much greenhouse gas as the average person in some countries generates in a year. Were fares to reflect that cost, many short trips would simply not be made, and the rail alternatives that already exist would become competitive. If we had priced carbon sooner, the train network would be in far better shape today, and we should not be debating whether it is possible to travel without flying.

The standard objection is that higher taxes punish ordinary families, who cannot afford to take holidays by any other means. It is a serious point, and I do not dismiss it. But a well-designed policy can answer it. Provided that revenue is returned to households, through lower rail fares for example, the poorest could end up better off. As long as the tax falls most heavily on frequent flyers, it also targets the minority that produces most of the aviation carbon footprint.

Should governments fail to act, the market will not act for them. Unless prices change, behaviour will not change either, and appeals to conscience have a poor record. Supposing every airline voluntarily doubled its fares tomorrow, it would lose customers to a rival; that is precisely why a rule must apply to all.

Nobody enjoys being told that a pleasure has become expensive. But there is a tipping point beyond which cheap becomes costly, and we are nearer to it than the weekend brochures suggest.

7.title: Review: a film adaptation of a novel
7.brief: An arts website has asked readers to review a film adaptation of a novel they have also read. Write a review in which you compare the film with the book, evaluate how successfully the adaptation captures the spirit of the original, and say whether you would recommend seeing the film, reading the book, or both.
7.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de una adaptación cinematográfica comparándola con la novela original.
criteria: Evaluative and critical vocabulary (understated, heavy-handed, luminous, a tour de force).
Intensifiers and downtoners used correctly with gradable and ungradable adjectives (utterly superb, slightly uneven, absolutely riveting).
Ellipsis and substitution to avoid repetition (so, not, do so, one).
Accurate adjective order and compound modifiers (a slow-burning, beautifully shot Irish drama).
7.model:
Quiet Waters: Faithful, Beautiful, and Slightly Too Polite

Adapting a novel as interior as 'Quiet Waters' was always going to be a risk. The book, a slow-burning account of two estranged sisters reunited at their mother's coastal house, takes place largely inside its narrator's head. Could a film possibly capture that? Surprisingly often, it does so.

Much of the credit belongs to the casting. As the elder sister, Clara, the lead gives an utterly compelling performance, conveying resentment and tenderness in a single glance. Her younger co-star is slightly less assured, though in fairness she has the thinner role; the novel's Ruth is a far more complex character than the film's. The cinematography, meanwhile, is luminous: long, grey-green shots of the Atlantic coastline do much of the work that the book's descriptive passages once did.

Where the adaptation falters is in its treatment of the novel's central secret. On the page, the revelation emerges gradually, through hints the reader may or may not notice. On screen, it is delivered in a rather heavy-handed flashback that explains far more than it needs to. I suspect the director feared audiences would miss the point; I think most would not. The result is a fairly conventional final act that lacks the book's devastating ambiguity.

There are smaller losses, too. The novel's wry humour has been almost entirely removed, leaving a film that is beautifully made but somewhat solemn. Readers who loved the sisters' sharp, affectionate bickering will miss it, and I certainly did.

Should you see it? Yes, particularly if you have not read the book, since the film stands perfectly well on its own. If you have, go anyway, but expect a respectful translation rather than a reinvention. Better still, read the novel first. It remains the richer of the two, and the film, for all its virtues, is a slightly too polite one.

7.title: Should the arts be publicly funded?
7.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — Culture as a public good
The arts do not merely entertain; they shape how a society understands itself. Public funding allows theatres, orchestras and galleries to take risks that the market would never support, and to remain accessible to people who could not otherwise afford them. Cities that invest in culture also benefit economically, attracting visitors and talent. To treat the arts as a luxury is to misunderstand their value entirely.

Text 2 — Who decides what is art?
When governments fund the arts, officials must decide which artists deserve support, and their choices inevitably reflect the tastes of a narrow, educated elite. Popular forms such as video games or stand-up comedy receive almost nothing, while opera, enjoyed by a small minority, absorbs enormous subsidies. If public money is to be spent on culture, it should follow what people actually value, not what experts believe they ought to.
7.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre la financiación pública de las artes.
criteria: Summaries of both texts that capture the main argument and supporting points.
Ellipsis and substitution (I believe so; the former does, the latter does not).
Gradable and ungradable adjectives with suitable modifiers.
Evaluative vocabulary of art and taste (elitist, accessible, highbrow, cultural value).
7.model:
The two texts address whether governments should fund the arts, the first defending public subsidy as essential and the second questioning who benefits from it.

The first writer contends that culture plays a fundamental role in how a society sees itself, and that state funding enables artistic institutions to experiment and to keep prices within reach of ordinary people. She adds that such investment also brings economic returns by drawing tourists and skilled workers. Her case is largely convincing, although the economic point is a slightly weaker one, implying that culture must justify itself commercially.

The second writer accepts the principle of public spending on culture but objects to the way decisions are made. In his view, funding bodies reflect the preferences of a highbrow minority, privileging forms such as opera while neglecting the entertainment most people actually enjoy. Public money, he concludes, ought to follow popular taste.

Is he right? Partly, I think. Funding bodies have undoubtedly been elitist at times, and there is no good reason why a ground-breaking video game should be considered less culturally valuable than an orchestral premiere. However, the suggestion that funding should simply mirror popularity is deeply problematic. Popular forms usually thrive in the market already; the former needs subsidy far less than the latter does. Public support exists precisely to sustain work that would not otherwise survive.

The most sensible approach, in my view, would combine the strengths of both arguments: continued investment in risk-taking and accessible art, decided by panels that are far more diverse than they have traditionally been. Should funding continue to be justified? I believe so, provided it serves the whole public rather than a privileged part of it.

7.title: Review: a debut poetry collection
7.brief: A literary review is publishing short reviews of recent poetry. Write a review of a collection of poems, real or imagined. Describe its themes and style, evaluate its strengths and weaknesses, and say whether you would recommend it and to whom.
7.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de un poemario, real o imaginado: temas, estilo, fortalezas, debilidades y a quién lo recomiendas.
criteria: Evaluative literary vocabulary (understated, luminous, heavy-handed, evocative, a tour de force).
Intensifiers and downtoners with gradable and ungradable adjectives (wonderfully assured, absolutely stunning, rather uneven, fairly conventional).
Ellipsis and substitution to avoid repetition (so, not, one, those who do not).
Correct adjective order and compound modifiers (a slim, beautifully produced volume; a long-awaited first collection).
7.model:
Small Hours, Large Silences

Isabel Moreno's long-awaited first collection, 'Small Hours', is a slim, beautifully produced volume of forty poems, most of them set in the sleepless period between midnight and dawn. It is a quietly devastating debut. The subjects are modest: a mother folding laundry, a night-shift nurse crossing a car park, a neighbour whose radio is never switched off. Moreno treats them with such restraint that the emotion arrives almost by accident, which is precisely how emotion tends to arrive in life.

The finest poems are wonderfully assured. 'Laundry', in which a daughter irons her dead mother's blouse, is absolutely stunning, and 'Car Park, 3 a.m.' is a tour de force of understatement, its final image, an unlocked car left running, impossible to forget. Moreno's language is plain and evocative; she never reaches for a grand adjective when a small, exact one will do. Her ear for rhythm is excellent, and the line breaks, always carefully judged, give her best work a luminous clarity.

The collection is, however, rather uneven. A group of poems in the middle section, about the sea, feels fairly conventional, and some of the images are heavy-handed: a lighthouse that stands for hope is one too many. The same could be said of the closing poem, whose moral is spelled out where silence would have served. One wishes the editor had been more severe, and perhaps the poet herself should have been so too.

Even so, the successes far outnumber the failures. Readers who admire Elizabeth Bishop or Wisława Szymborska will find much to enjoy here, and those who do not yet know either may find the best way in. Is it for everyone? Hardly; it demands patience, and those who like their poetry loud will not. But anyone willing to sit up late with a small book of good poems will be richly rewarded.

7.title: Walls that talk back: street art and the ownership of space
7.brief: An arts journal is publishing critical essays on contested forms of culture. Write a critical essay on whether street art should be regarded as vandalism or as legitimate public art, considering who owns public space and who decides what counts as art.
7.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo crítico sobre si el arte callejero es vandalismo o arte público legítimo: quién es dueño del espacio público y quién decide qué es arte.
criteria: Evaluative and critical vocabulary (subversive, ephemeral, derivative, striking, accessible).
Intensifiers and downtoners used accurately (utterly pointless, fairly reasonable, absolutely fascinating).
Ellipsis and substitution (so, not, do so, the former / the latter, one, those).
Correct adjective order and compound modifiers (a vividly painted, six-metre-high mural).
7.model:
Walls That Talk Back: Street Art and the Ownership of Space

A vividly painted, six-metre-high mural of a river dolphin appeared overnight on the side of a disused warehouse in my city, and the debate that followed was entirely predictable. Half of the neighbours called it vandalism; the other half called it art. I suspect that both were right, which is why the question deserves more than a slogan.

The case against street art rests on property. A wall belongs to someone, and painting it without permission is, in law, an offence. That is a fairly reasonable position, and nobody should dismiss it lightly: the owner of a small shop has every right to object to graffiti on the shutters. Yet the argument proves less than it appears to. Much of the public wall space in cities is neglected, anonymous and ugly, and one wonders who exactly is being deprived when it is made beautiful. Should owners be consulted? Ideally so, but not always.

The case in favour is that street art does what galleries cannot: it reaches people who would never visit one. It is ephemeral, accessible and often subversive, absolutely fascinating when it comments on the neighbourhood around it and utterly pointless when it merely repeats a famous name. Much of it is derivative; some of it is striking; the best is both local and original. The same range of quality can be found in any gallery, and nobody proposes to abolish those.

The real question is who decides. Councils may commission murals, and many already do; the former approach is orderly but risks losing the spontaneity that gives the form its energy, whereas the latter has energy but little accountability. A sensible compromise might be a number of legal walls in every district, so that artists can paint without fear and communities can remove work they find offensive.

Street art is not always vandalism, nor is it always art. It is a conversation, and like any conversation it should be judged on what is said, not simply on whether permission was asked first.

7.title: Let them be sad
7.brief: A culture magazine is asking readers to defend unpopular tastes. Write an opinion article arguing that stories (novels, films or series) with unhappy or unresolved endings deserve more respect than they get, using examples.
7.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de opinión que defienda los finales tristes o abiertos en novelas, películas o series, con ejemplos.
criteria: Evaluative vocabulary of storytelling (heavy-handed, slow-burning, devastating, inevitable).
Intensifiers and downtoners with gradable and ungradable adjectives (utterly brilliant, rather predictable, somewhat disappointing, absolutely devastating).
Ellipsis and substitution (some are, I think not, do so, a sad one, the best ones).
Accurate adjective order and compound modifiers (a slow-burning, quietly moving, award-winning Japanese drama).
7.model:
Let Them Be Sad

At the end of a film I once adored, a couple who have spent two hours falling in love fail to meet at the train station, and the credits roll. The cinema, I remember, groaned. A woman behind me said it was a cheat. I thought it the bravest thing the director could have done, and I want to defend the unhappy ending against the people who find it somewhat disappointing.

Happy endings are, of course, perfectly respectable. Many are well earned, and some are utterly brilliant. But the form has a habit of becoming rather predictable, especially in a market that has learned that audiences like to leave smiling. When every story resolves, none can surprise us, and we begin to treat narrative as a delivery system for reassurance. The unhappy ending reminds us that fiction can do something harder: it can tell the truth about loss.

Consider a slow-burning, quietly moving, award-winning Japanese drama I saw last year, in which an elderly widower never learns what became of his son. Nothing is resolved; the final scene shows him laying two places at the table, as he always did. It was absolutely devastating, and it has stayed with me far longer than many tidier films I enjoyed more at the time. A happy ending is a pleasure to watch, and a sad one is a pleasure to remember.

Critics of the unresolved ending say that it is lazy, and some are, I admit. A heavy-handed tragedy that kills off a character for effect is no braver than a heavy-handed rescue. But the best ones do not feel arbitrary; they feel inevitable, which is the highest compliment one can pay a story.

Do we need our fiction to comfort us? Occasionally, yes. Do we need it to do so every time? I think not. A culture that can only bear happy endings is, I suspect, not very confident in its own resilience.

7.title: Save the Cine Rex
7.brief: The independent cinema in your town is to be demolished to make way for flats. Write a formal persuasive letter to the council's head of culture urging them to protect the building, arguing for its cultural value and proposing a practical way forward.
7.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal persuasiva a la jefa de cultura del ayuntamiento para salvar un cine independiente de la demolición, con una propuesta práctica.
criteria: Formal letter conventions and a clear request.
Evaluative vocabulary (irreplaceable, run-down, characterful, thriving, a landmark).
Intensifiers and downtoners used accurately (utterly irreplaceable, slightly dated, fairly modest).

Ellipsis and substitution (I do so, whether it is so, as other towns have done, a cinema like the Rex cannot) and correct adjective order with compound modifiers (a beautifully preserved, 1930s Art Deco building).
7.model:
Dear Ms Alvarado,

I am writing to ask the Council to reconsider the planned demolition of the Cine Rex on Calle Bolívar, and to explore ways of protecting it. I do so as a resident of forty years and as a volunteer who has helped to run its film club for the last eight.

The Rex is a beautifully preserved, 1930s Art Deco building, and it is utterly irreplaceable. Its façade is a landmark that appears on postcards, and its single screen has shown films to four generations of local families. The interior is slightly dated, certainly, and the seats could do with replacing; but a run-down building is not the same as a worthless one, and this one has a rare, characterful atmosphere that no multiplex can offer.

I recognise that the town needs housing, and I would not suggest otherwise. Yet the demolition is being presented as inevitable, and I would respectfully question whether it is so. Several empty sites nearer the station are fairly suitable for flats; none of them has a history. The cinema, by contrast, is a thriving cultural space: its Saturday matinees for children are almost always full, and its film club has more than two hundred members.

I would therefore like to propose a practical alternative. The Council might list the building as a cultural asset, which would delay demolition while a study is carried out. It could then invite the community to form a trust to run the cinema, as other towns have done, with a fairly modest grant to cover essential repairs. The owner, who is understandably cautious, may be willing to sell at a reasonable price; if not, a compulsory purchase would be a last resort.

Places like this, once lost, are not recovered. A new block of flats can be built anywhere, but a cinema like the Rex cannot. I would be grateful for the opportunity to meet you to discuss how the community might help.

Yours sincerely,

Julián Cárdenas

8.title: Does protest still work?
8.brief: An online current affairs magazine has invited articles answering the question: 'Does protest still change anything?'. Write an article in which you consider examples of protest, past or present, assess what makes some protests effective and others not, and give your own view.
8.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para una revista de actualidad sobre si las protestas siguen cambiando algo.
criteria: A thought-provoking title and opening, and a confident, persuasive voice.
Unreal past forms (I wish, if only, it's high time, would rather, as if).
Concession and contrast (albeit, notwithstanding, much as, however + adjective).
Vocabulary of politics, protest and change (grassroots, civil disobedience, to mobilise, to concede).
8.model:
Marching On: Why Protest Still Matters

Every few years, a crowd fills the streets, the cameras arrive, and commentators announce that nothing will change. Sometimes they are right. Much as we might wish otherwise, most marches end with tired feet and an unchanged policy. Yet if protest were truly pointless, governments would hardly spend so much effort trying to restrict it.

History suggests that protest works, albeit slowly and rarely in the way participants expect. The campaigns for women's suffrage, civil rights and workers' protections were each dismissed in their day as noisy, naive or dangerous. None succeeded through a single demonstration. What they had in common was persistence: years of grassroots organising, boycotts, petitions and, at times, civil disobedience, until those in power concluded that conceding was less costly than resisting.

The protests that fade, by contrast, tend to share a different pattern. They mobilise enormous numbers for a day, then disappear, as if attendance alone were the objective. However impressive the crowd, a government that can wait for it to go home usually will. Effective movements, notwithstanding their diversity, know exactly what they are asking for and keep asking long after the headlines have moved on.

There is a further ingredient: broad support. Movements that alienate the public, however just their cause, give their opponents an easy target. I would rather see a campaign win over a sceptical neighbour than shock a city for an afternoon, although the two are not always incompatible.

So does protest still change things? Yes, but not on its own. If only more of us understood that a march is the beginning of a campaign rather than its climax, fewer people would walk away disappointed. It's high time we stopped asking whether protest works and started asking what it takes to make it work. The answer, inconveniently, is patience.

8.title: Should voting be compulsory?
8.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — A civic duty
In countries where voting is compulsory, turnout routinely exceeds ninety per cent, and governments must therefore appeal to the whole population rather than to the most motivated groups. The obligation is light: a short trip to a polling station once every few years, with the option of spoiling one's ballot. It is essential that every citizen take part if democracy is to represent everyone, not merely the comfortable and the committed.

Text 2 — The freedom not to choose
Democracy rests on freedom, and that must include the freedom to abstain. Forcing reluctant citizens to vote adds millions of uninformed or random choices to the count, which hardly improves the quality of decisions. Low turnout is a symptom of disillusionment; the remedy is to give people reasons to vote, not to fine them for staying at home.
8.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre el voto obligatorio.
criteria: Balanced summaries using precise reporting verbs.
The subjunctive after verbs and adjectives of necessity (essential that every citizen take part, insist that the state not…).
Concessive structures (albeit, much as, notwithstanding).
Political and legal vocabulary (turnout, abstain, spoiled ballot, disenfranchised).
8.model:
Both texts debate whether citizens should be legally required to vote, but they disagree fundamentally about what democracy demands.

The first text argues that compulsory voting produces near-universal turnout and therefore obliges politicians to address the interests of the entire electorate rather than only its most active sections. Its author stresses that the burden is minimal, particularly since voters may still submit a blank or spoiled ballot, and insists that universal participation be regarded as a precondition of genuinely representative government. This is a strong argument: in many countries, the young and the poor vote far less than the old and the affluent, and policy inevitably reflects this.

The second text maintains that freedom in a democracy includes the right not to participate. Its writer suggests that compelling unwilling voters merely adds uninformed choices to the result, and that falling turnout should be treated as a warning sign of disillusionment, to be addressed by making politics more meaningful rather than by penalising abstention.

Much as I sympathise with the second writer's defence of liberty, I find the first argument more persuasive. The 'freedom' to abstain is exercised disproportionately by those who already feel disenfranchised, and its effect is to make their exclusion permanent. Moreover, the obligation to attend a polling station, albeit a genuine restriction, is a modest one compared with other civic duties such as jury service. Notwithstanding the genuine concern about uninformed choices, the same objection applies to many voters under voluntary systems. Ideally, compulsion would go hand in hand with the reforms the second writer recommends, so that citizens are not only required to vote but given good reason to want to.

8.title: Votes at sixteen
8.brief: You are the first speaker for the proposition in a school debating final on the motion 'This house would lower the voting age to sixteen'. Write your constructive speech (about three minutes).
8.briefEs: Escribe el discurso inicial de la proposición en una final de debate escolar sobre bajar la edad de voto a dieciséis años.
criteria: Direct address to the chair, the opposition and the audience, a clear structure and a strong close.
At least two uses of the mandative subjunctive (the voting age be lowered, every citizen have…).
Unreal past forms (it is time we stopped…, as if they were, I would rather we…, if only, I wish).
Concessive structures (albeit, much as, notwithstanding, however + adjective) and political vocabulary (franchise, turnout, to abstain).
8.model:
Madam Chair, honourable opponents, ladies and gentlemen,

We stand here to propose that the voting age be lowered to sixteen, and I would like to begin by saying what we are not proposing. We do not claim that sixteen-year-olds are wiser than their elders. We claim only that they are citizens, and that citizens should have a say.

Consider the facts. A sixteen-year-old may work, pay tax and in many countries join the armed forces, yet has no voice in the decisions that govern all three. It is time we stopped treating them as if they were children when the burden falls and as adults when it suits us. Much as the opposition may wish to protect young people from politics, politics will not stop affecting them, and it is essential that every citizen who contributes to society have the chance to shape it.

The opposition will say that sixteen-year-olds lack experience. Albeit a fair concern, it proves too much: experience is not a condition of the franchise at any other age. Nobody asks an eighty-year-old to demonstrate understanding before voting. Notwithstanding their youth, the sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds who were allowed to vote in Scotland's referendum turned out in impressive numbers.

There is a longer-term argument too. Voting is a habit, and habits form early. I would rather we enfranchised young people while they are still at school, where they can discuss the issues in class, than leave them to abstain at eighteen, newly independent and unsure. If only we had begun this experiment a generation ago, our turnout figures might be healthier today, and I wish more of my own generation had been introduced to the ballot earlier.

We propose, therefore, that the voting age be lowered, that schools provide civic education beforehand, and that the first election be treated as a lesson, not a test. However sceptical you may be, I urge you to give the next generation the trust it has already earned.

Thank you.

8.title: Protecting those who speak out
8.brief: A well-known case has shown that employees who reveal wrongdoing in their organisations can lose their jobs and reputations. Write a formal persuasive letter to your Member of Parliament urging stronger legal protection for whistleblowers.
8.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal persuasiva a tu representante parlamentario pidiendo mayor protección legal para los denunciantes de irregularidades.
criteria: Formal letter conventions and a clear request.
Mandative subjunctive (I urge that the burden of proof be shifted, it is essential that a whistleblower not be dismissed).
Unreal past forms (it is high time that…, I wish… would, if only, I would rather).
Concessive structures (albeit, notwithstanding, much as, however + adjective) and legal vocabulary (disclosure, retaliation, legislation).
8.model:
Dear Mr Okonkwo,

I am writing as a constituent to urge you to support stronger legal protection for whistleblowers, and to ask that you raise the matter when the relevant bill returns to the House next month.

The recent case of a hospital administrator who reported unsafe staffing levels is, I believe, a warning. She was suspended within a fortnight, and her career has not recovered. It is high time that Parliament recognised that a system in which honesty is punished is a system designed to protect those who do wrong. I wish more legislators would consider what such cases tell other employees: that silence is safe, and disclosure is dangerous.

The existing law is inadequate. Protection exists on paper, but workers must prove that they suffered retaliation because of their disclosure, a burden that is nearly impossible to meet against an employer with experienced lawyers. Much as I respect the principle of employers' confidentiality, it cannot justify concealing risks to public safety. Notwithstanding the efforts of some conscientious organisations, voluntary good practice has plainly failed.

I would therefore ask that you press for three amendments. First, I urge that the burden of proof be shifted to the employer once a disclosure has been made. Second, it is essential that a whistleblower not be dismissed or demoted while an investigation is under way. Third, I propose that an independent body be established to hear complaints swiftly, so that workers need not wait years for justice.

Some will object that such measures invite malicious reports. That is a legitimate worry, albeit an exaggerated one: the law can distinguish between a good-faith report and a vindictive one, and it already does so in other areas. However reasonable the concern, it should not be allowed to paralyse reform.

If only the hospital had listened, the harm might have been averted at much lower cost. I would rather we learnt from this case than repeated it. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Yours sincerely,

Helena Ruiz

8.title: Punishment or second chance? The purpose of prison
8.brief: A law and society journal invites critical essays on punishment. Write an essay evaluating whether the main aim of prison sentences should be punishment or rehabilitation, weighing arguments on both sides and reaching a reasoned conclusion.
8.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo crítico sobre si el objetivo principal de la prisión debe ser castigar o rehabilitar, sopesando ambas posturas.
criteria: A mandative subjunctive or formal necessity structure (it is essential that programmes be funded, insist that the state take…).
Unreal past forms (as if society were…, I would rather we invested…, it is time we recognised…).
At least three concessive structures (although, much as, notwithstanding, albeit, however + adjective).
Legal vocabulary (retribution, deterrence, reoffending, parole) and a balanced conclusion.
8.model:
Punishment or Second Chance? The Purpose of Prison

Every society must decide what a prison sentence is for. Is it retribution, deterrence, protection of the public or the remaking of the offender? The answer determines how prisons are run, and it explains why so many of them, in practice, do none of these things well. This essay argues that although punishment has a legitimate place, rehabilitation ought to be the principal aim.

The case for punishment should not be dismissed. Much as we may wish to believe that people are shaped entirely by circumstance, there is a moral intuition, widely shared, that serious wrongdoing deserves a proportionate response. It is reasonable to insist that the state take such feelings seriously, and a system that appeared indifferent to them would soon lose public trust.

The difficulty is that punishment as an end in itself does not appear to work. Notwithstanding its intuitive appeal, deterrence is weak: those who commit crimes seldom expect to be caught, and the severity of a sentence matters far less than the likelihood of detection. Worse, long sentences served in overcrowded conditions often leave prisoners less employable and more embittered, which raises rates of reoffending. It is as if society were paying a high price to manufacture the very problem it hopes to solve.

By contrast, programmes offering education, therapy and work experience have been associated with lower reoffending, albeit with variations across countries. It is essential that such programmes be properly funded and that release on parole be accompanied by genuine support for housing and employment. I would rather we invested in these measures than in additional cells.

However attractive retribution may be, it cannot be the foundation of a sensible policy. Punishment will continue to have a place in sentencing; but it is time we recognised that a prison which sends people back into society worse than it found them has failed everyone, including those it was meant to avenge.

8.title: The day I said nothing
8.brief: A magazine invites readers to reflect on moments when they failed to act on their principles. Write a reflective essay about a time you stayed silent when you should have spoken, what you wish you had done, and what you would do differently now.
8.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo reflexivo sobre una ocasión en que callaste cuando debías hablar, lo que desearías haber hecho y lo que harías hoy.
criteria: Unreal past forms: wish + past perfect, wish + would, and if only or as if.
At least one mandative subjunctive or formal necessity structure (it was essential that the criticism be directed…, I insisted that I be…).
Concessive structures (albeit, much as, however + verb, notwithstanding).
Vocabulary of justice and conscience (complicit, to speak up, accountable, to turn a blind eye).
8.model:
The Day I Said Nothing

I have rehearsed the scene so many times that I can no longer be sure how it really went. A colleague, whom I will call Daniel, was being mocked in a meeting by our manager for a mistake that was not his. The remarks were small and cruel, and the laughter that followed was the nervous kind. I sat there with my notes in front of me, knowing precisely who had made the error, because it was me.

I wish I had spoken up. I wish I had said, in a calm voice, that the fault was mine and that it was essential that the criticism be directed where it belonged. Instead I looked at the table. Much as I would like to believe that I was merely confused, the truth is that I was frightened of the consequences, and I turned a blind eye to Daniel's embarrassment as if it were not my concern. However you describe it, I was complicit.

What makes it worse is that nobody noticed. Daniel never learned that I could have saved him, and the manager, I suppose, never thought of it again. If only I had understood then that silence is rarely neutral, I might have acted differently. It is a poor consolation that most of us, at one time or another, have behaved in exactly the same way.

Notwithstanding the discomfort, I did eventually act, albeit weeks late. I told Daniel what had happened and apologised. He was gracious about it, which was almost harder to bear than anger. I also insisted to myself that I be more careful in future, and I have tried to keep that promise by speaking early, even when my voice shakes.

I still wish the manager would apologise to Daniel, though I know he never will. What I can control is my own conduct: to hold myself accountable, and to speak up, quickly and plainly, the next time someone is blamed for a mistake that is mine.

9.title: Report on staff wellbeing
9.brief: The management of the company where you work introduced a wellbeing programme six months ago, including flexible hours, a lunchtime exercise class and access to a counselling service. You have been asked to write a report for senior managers assessing how far the programme has met its aims and recommending improvements.
9.briefEs: Escribe un informe para la dirección evaluando un programa de bienestar laboral y proponiendo mejoras.
criteria: Report layout with headings, impersonal and objective style.
Discourse markers and cohesive devices at C2 (that said, by the same token, in light of, to this end).
Future in the past (was to be reviewed, was about to be withdrawn, would later prove).
Precise prepositional and phrasal verbs in formal register (account for, draw on, phase in, call for).
9.model:
Purpose
This report assesses the staff wellbeing programme introduced in March, which was to be reviewed after six months. It draws on an anonymous survey completed by 148 employees, together with attendance figures supplied by Human Resources.

Flexible working
This has been by far the most successful element. Some 82% of respondents reported that flexible hours had reduced stress, particularly among staff with caring responsibilities. Sickness absence fell by approximately 15% over the period, a reduction which, in light of the survey results, can reasonably be attributed at least in part to the new arrangements. That said, a minority of team leaders expressed concern about coordinating meetings, and clearer guidelines appear to be needed.

Exercise classes
Attendance was initially high but declined steadily, falling to an average of six participants per session by August. Respondents accounted for this mainly by citing the timing: a lunchtime class left insufficient time to eat and change. Interestingly, several staff members suggested that a walking group would appeal to colleagues who are put off by formal exercise.

Counselling service
Usage figures were low, but the survey suggests this does not reflect a lack of need. Many respondents were unaware that the service existed, and others feared that using it would be noted by managers. By the same token, those who had used it rated it highly.

Recommendations
To this end, the following measures are recommended:
• the publication of guidelines on flexible working for team leaders;
• replacing the lunchtime class with a choice of early-morning sessions and an informal walking group;
• a communications campaign emphasising the confidentiality of the counselling service.

Conclusion
The exercise class, which was at one point about to be withdrawn, may yet prove worthwhile in a revised format. Overall, the programme has made a promising start, and the changes proposed should be phased in before the next review in March.

9.title: Risk in childhood play
9.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — The value of scraped knees
Children who climb trees, build dens and play unsupervised learn to judge danger for themselves. Over-protective rules, by removing every possible hazard from playgrounds and schools, deprive them of the chance to develop resilience and confidence. Research suggests that children allowed moderate risk in play are, if anything, less likely to be seriously injured later, because they have learned their own limits.

Text 2 — Safety is not paranoia
It is easy to mock safety rules until a child is badly hurt. Playground standards were introduced for good reasons, and the injuries they prevent are real. Moreover, the world children grow up in has changed: traffic is heavier, and parents who let children roam freely may face criticism or worse. Encouraging risk sounds bold, but it is parents and teachers who will bear the consequences when things go wrong.
9.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre el riesgo en el juego infantil.
criteria: Faithful summaries of both texts.
Discourse markers and cohesive devices beyond the basics (that said, by contrast, it follows that, admittedly).
Risk collocations (calculated risk, run the risk of, mitigate a risk, risk-averse).
A nuanced personal conclusion.
9.model:
The two texts consider how much risk children should be allowed in play, the first arguing for greater freedom and the second defending existing safety measures.

According to the first writer, activities such as climbing and unsupervised play enable children to assess danger independently, and excessive caution robs them of opportunities to build confidence and resilience. He cites research indicating that children exposed to moderate risks may in fact be less prone to serious injury later, having learned what they are capable of. This is a persuasive claim, and it chimes with the experience of many adults who remember their own childhood adventures fondly.

The second writer, by contrast, warns against dismissing safety regulations, which she points out were introduced in response to genuine harm. She also argues that circumstances have changed, with busier roads and greater social pressure on parents, and stresses that those who encourage risk-taking are rarely the ones held responsible when accidents occur.

Admittedly, the second text raises a fair point about accountability; it is easy to champion risk when one does not bear its consequences. That said, the two positions are less opposed than they appear. What the first writer advocates is not recklessness but a calculated risk, the kind of manageable challenge that allows children to learn without running the risk of serious harm. It follows that the aim should be to mitigate genuinely dangerous hazards, such as traffic, while tolerating minor ones, such as scraped knees. A society so risk-averse that children never fall may find it has raised adults who are afraid to climb at all.

9.title: Executive report: injuries at Riverside Sports Club
9.brief: A community sports club has recorded a rise in injuries since it introduced a new training schedule. Write an executive report for the committee analysing the causes, evaluating the options and recommending actions.
9.briefEs: Escribe un informe ejecutivo para el comité de un club deportivo sobre el aumento de lesiones tras un nuevo horario de entrenamiento: causas, opciones y recomendaciones.
criteria: Report layout with headings and an objective, impersonal tone.
Future in the past (was to be reviewed, was due to take place, was about to be cancelled, would later prove).
At least three C2 discourse markers (that said, by the same token, in light of, to this end, as a result).
Formal and prepositional verbs (attribute to, account for, draw attention to, phase in).
9.model:
Executive Report: Injuries at Riverside Sports Club

Summary
This report examines the increase in injuries recorded since the introduction of the new training schedule in September, which was to be reviewed after one term. The analysis draws on the club's injury log and on interviews with six coaches. In light of the findings, it recommends that the schedule be modified rather than withdrawn.

Findings
The number of reported injuries rose from nine in the previous spring term to twenty-three this term. Most of the increase can be attributed to the extra Thursday session, which was introduced to prepare players for a tournament that was due to take place in December. The tournament, which was about to be cancelled owing to a lack of teams, eventually went ahead, but the additional training would later prove to have been unnecessary for the majority of members. Interviews with coaches draw attention to a further factor: the rapid increase in training load, with little time for recovery between sessions. Furthermore, a survey of fifty players showed that nearly half had felt fatigued during sessions, and several had continued to train despite minor pain. That said, the club's pitch maintenance, which was initially suspected, does not appear to account for the rise.

Implications
By the same token, the new schedule has had benefits. Attendance has risen by 20 per cent, and several newer members have reported feeling more confident. It would therefore be counter-productive to abandon the scheme altogether. Nevertheless, the data call for a more cautious approach, particularly for players under sixteen.

Recommendations
To this end, the committee is advised to:
• remove the Thursday session for players under sixteen;
• phase in any increase in training load over six weeks;
• appoint a qualified first-aider to monitor injuries and report to the committee each month.
A further review should be carried out at the end of the spring term, and, as a result, any necessary adjustments could be made before the next season.

9.title: Courage or recklessness?
9.brief: A lifestyle magazine is asking readers whether people who take part in extreme sports are courageous or reckless. Write an opinion article that takes a position, considers the risks to the individual and to others, and says whether society should discourage such activities.
9.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de opinión sobre si quienes practican deportes extremos son valientes o temerarios, con una postura clara y atención a los riesgos.
criteria: Future in the past (I was about to attempt, as I would later realise, was to prove).
At least three C2 discourse markers (admittedly, that said, by the same token, in light of, to this end, all the same).
Formal prepositional and phrasal verbs (take on, draw on, account for, weigh up, call for).
Vocabulary of risk (hazard, calculated risk, reckless) and a position that avoids sweeping generalisation.
9.model:
Courage or Recklessness?

On the morning I was about to attempt my first parachute jump, the instructor asked me a question I have never forgotten: 'Do you want to know the odds?' I said no. It was the wrong answer, and, as I would later realise, the one most of us give when risk becomes exciting.

Admittedly, the case against extreme sports is easy to make. Climbers, base jumpers and big-wave surfers do die, and their deaths can seem pointlessly avoidable. Those who take on such challenges are often accused of selfishness, since rescue services, families and friends bear the consequences. That said, the accusation oversimplifies. Most participants are highly trained, and their activities draw on years of preparation, equipment checks and rehearsed contingencies. What looks from outside like a reckless gamble is frequently a carefully calculated risk.

By the same token, we should not romanticise danger. Some deaths can be accounted for by overconfidence, social-media pressure or ignorance of conditions. In light of this, the distinction that matters is not between safe and dangerous activities, but between informed and uninformed risk. A person who has weighed up the hazards and accepted them is behaving very differently from one who has been dared.

What, then, should society do? I do not think it calls for prohibition. Many ordinary activities, from driving to smoking, carry greater risk, and we do not ban them. To this end, the sensible response is to regulate instructors, require insurance and make honest information available. All the same, communities that fund mountain rescue have every right to ask participants to contribute.

My own jump, incidentally, went perfectly well. The experience was to prove less terrifying than the waiting. But I know now what the instructor meant: courage is not the absence of knowledge, but the decision to act upon it.

9.title: Wellness: science, sales or both?
9.brief: A magazine of science and society is publishing critical essays on consumer culture. Write a critical essay on the wellness industry (supplements, detox diets, retreats): how much of it is supported by evidence, why it is so popular and how consumers should approach it.
9.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo crítico sobre la industria del bienestar (suplementos, dietas detox, retiros): qué respalda la evidencia, por qué es popular y cómo debe abordarla el consumidor.
criteria: Future in the past (was about to fail, was to become, would later turn out).
At least three C2 discourse markers (admittedly, by the same token, that said, in light of, to this end, nonetheless).
Formal and prepositional verbs (stem from, draw on, lend itself to, call for, account for).
Appropriate hedging, concrete examples and a critical but fair stance.
9.model:
Wellness: Science, Sales or Both?

When the first juice-cleanse shop opened on our street, I assumed it was about to fail. It was to become a chain of eleven. The wellness industry, now worth many billions worldwide, has proved me wrong in this and in a good many other predictions, and its success calls for explanation.

Part of it stems from a genuine need. Modern life is stressful, health systems are overstretched, and people want to feel that they have some control over their own wellbeing. Admittedly, some of what the industry promotes, such as sleep hygiene, exercise and time outdoors, draws on solid evidence. By the same token, it would be unfair to ridicule everyone who seeks help from a yoga class or a meditation app.

That said, much of the sector lends itself to exaggeration. 'Detox' regimes are the clearest example: healthy kidneys and a healthy liver already remove toxins from the body, and no convincing study I know of has shown that a juice cleanse does so more effectively. A few supplements are useful for people with specific deficiencies; many are taken by people who have none, on the strength of testimonials rather than trials. In light of this, claims that a product will 'boost immunity' should be treated with caution, if not suspicion.

Why, then, does the industry thrive? Partly because its promises are unfalsifiable. If you feel better after a retreat, the retreat worked; if you do not, you were not committed enough. The scepticism that the same consumers would apply to a used car is suspended, and what might otherwise be dismissed as sales talk is accepted as advice.

To this end, I would suggest three questions before buying anything. Who profits if I believe this? What evidence, other than testimonials, supports it? And would it cost less to ask a doctor? Nonetheless, I would not wish to dismiss the instinct behind the industry. The desire to look after oneself is healthy; it simply needs better information than it is currently given.

9.title: A room, a ramp and a kind person
9.brief: You have been asked to speak at a fundraising dinner for a new paediatric rehabilitation unit at a local hospital. Write a speech in which you describe what the unit will mean for local families and persuade guests to give generously.
9.briefEs: Escribe un discurso para una cena benéfica que recauda fondos para una unidad de rehabilitación infantil: qué significará para las familias y por qué donar.
criteria: Direct address, a personal opening and a clear call to action.
Future in the past (was about to begin, was to become, we were about to give up).
At least three C2 discourse markers (admittedly, that said, by the same token, in light of, to this end, all the same).
Formal and prepositional verbs (call for, rely on, draw on, bring about).
9.model:
Good evening, ladies and gentlemen, and thank you for coming.

Five years ago, I was sitting in a corridor of this hospital with my daughter, who was about to begin the first of many rehabilitation sessions after an accident. The therapy she needed was available only in the capital, a six-hour journey away. We were about to give up, and then a physiotherapist, whose name I will never forget, said: 'There is a room we can use.' It was a storeroom. It was to become, for eleven months, the best place in the world.

That room is the reason we are all here tonight. In light of the demand, the hospital is planning a proper paediatric rehabilitation unit, and it calls for your help. Admittedly, it is a large project. It will need specialist equipment, trained staff and a building adapted for children who are learning, once again, to walk, to grip a pencil or to speak.

That said, the numbers should encourage you. Every donation made tonight will be matched by the regional government, and the unit will rely on volunteers for much of its everyday work. By the same token, the money does not vanish: over the next ten years, the unit is expected to treat more than two thousand children who would otherwise have had to travel.

To this end, I ask you to be generous, and I ask it without apology. Think of a parent drawing on every reserve of strength, and of how much easier it would be with a room, a ramp and a kind person nearby. All the same, I do not wish to pressure anyone; give what you can, and give gladly.

My daughter, now fourteen, runs for her school. She tells me now that she remembers little of the storeroom, only the encouragement. Tonight, you have the chance to give that to two thousand other children. Thank you.

10.title: Preserving the past or building the future?
10.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — Heritage as identity
Historic buildings and old neighbourhoods are more than bricks and mortar; they are the visible memory of a community. Once demolished, they can never be replaced, and the generic towers that succeed them could stand in any city in the world. Protecting heritage is not nostalgia but a way of ensuring that future generations inherit places with character, history and a sense of belonging.

Text 2 — Cities must change
Cities have always grown by replacing the old with the new; the 'historic' quarters we treasure today were once controversial developments themselves. Excessive protection freezes cities in time, drives up housing costs and prevents the construction of the homes that young people desperately need. A city that cannot change is on the verge of becoming a museum, admired by visitors but unaffordable for its residents.
10.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre la conservación del patrimonio frente a la necesidad de vivienda nueva.
criteria: Concise summaries of both texts in your own words.
Advanced future forms (will have been, is to be, is on the verge of, is due to).
Comparative structures with nuance (the more…the more, nowhere near as, every bit as).
At least one proverb or fixed expression used appropriately in a formal register.
10.model:
The two texts consider the tension between conserving historic urban environments and allowing cities to develop, the first prioritising heritage and the second the need for change.

The first writer argues that old buildings embody a community's collective memory and that their loss is irreversible. Their replacements, she suggests, are often anonymous structures with nowhere near as much character, and protecting heritage is therefore a means of passing on distinctive places to future generations. The argument is a powerful one; most of us can think of a beloved street that was swept away for a development which nobody now admires.

The second writer counters that renewal has always been the norm, pointing out that districts now considered historic were themselves once new. He maintains that over-protection prevents cities from adapting, raises rents and blocks the construction of much-needed housing, warning that a city that cannot change risks becoming a showpiece that its own residents can no longer afford.

In my view, both writers are right about different things. Heritage is every bit as valuable as the first text claims, yet the second is correct that preservation can become an excuse for inaction. The more rigidly we protect entire districts, the more we push development, and young people, elsewhere. A sensible approach would distinguish between buildings of genuine significance and those that are merely old. By the middle of this century, many cities will have been struggling with housing shortages for decades, and Rome, as the saying goes, was not built in a day. It would be unwise, however, to forget that it was not preserved in one either.

10.title: What will we be remembered for?
10.brief: A magazine is publishing a special issue on the theme of legacy. Write an article responding to the question 'What will our generation be remembered for?'. You should consider both the achievements and the failures that future generations might associate with us, and reflect on what kind of legacy we should be trying to leave.
10.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para un número especial sobre el legado: ¿por qué será recordada nuestra generación?
criteria: An engaging title and a reflective, personal yet polished voice.
Advanced future forms (by 2080 historians will have been…, we are on the verge of, is due to).
Nuanced comparatives (every bit as, nowhere near, the sooner…the better).
Proverbs and fixed expressions used naturally (time will tell, actions speak louder than words).
10.model:
Dear Future: A Note on What We Left You

Somewhere around the year 2080, a historian is due to write the definitive account of our era. By then, she will have been sifting through our digital debris for years: billions of photographs, an ocean of messages, and a staggering quantity of videos of cats. What, I wonder, will she conclude?

She may well be impressed. We are, after all, the generation that sequenced genomes in hours, connected almost every corner of the planet and developed vaccines faster than anyone thought possible. We are on the verge of breakthroughs in clean energy that our grandparents would have dismissed as fantasy. In many respects, we have been every bit as inventive as any generation before us.

Yet I suspect our historian will be nowhere near as forgiving about other matters. She will note that we understood, in detail, what our emissions were doing to the climate, and that for decades we carried on regardless. She will notice that we had the means to reduce poverty dramatically and chose, too often, to look away. Actions, as the saying goes, speak louder than words, and our words were frequently eloquent.

So what legacy should we be aiming for? Not perfection, which no generation achieves, but something more modest: a world left with more options than we found it, not fewer. That means forests still standing, languages still spoken, institutions still trusted. It means making decisions whose benefits we may never live to enjoy, which is, perhaps, the truest test of whether we are thinking about the future at all.
