Time will tell whether we rise to the occasion. But the sooner we begin to act as though our historian is watching, the kinder her verdict is likely to be. And unlike most authors, we still have the chance to change the ending of our own story.

10.title: What we hand down
10.brief: A magazine is publishing reflective essays under the heading 'What we hand down'. Write a reflective essay about something you have inherited, whether an object, a skill or a belief, and what you hope to pass on to the people who come after you.
10.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo reflexivo sobre algo que has heredado (un objeto, una habilidad, una creencia) y lo que esperas transmitir a quienes vienen después.
criteria: Advanced future forms (will have been practising, is due in March, is on the verge of, by the time).
Nuanced comparatives (the more… the more, every bit as, nowhere near as, by far the).
At least one proverb or fixed expression used naturally (the apple does not fall far from the tree, actions speak louder than words, time will tell).
A reflective, personal voice and a closing sentence that looks forward.
10.model:
What We Hand Down

My grandfather left me a hammer. It is not a valuable object: the handle has been replaced twice, the head is dented, and it is nowhere near as elegant as the tools in the shop where I bought my own. But it is, by far, the most precious thing I own, and I have been wondering lately what it is that I am actually inheriting.

The easy answer is a skill. By the time he was my age, my grandfather had built three houses with it, one of them the house in which my mother grew up. The more I use the hammer, the more I understand how little of the skill lives in the tool. It lives in the wrist, in a patience that cannot be bought. Every bit as important, I now think, was his attitude to mistakes. He would examine a crooked nail with real interest, as if it were telling him something, and then he would simply start again.

People say that the apple does not fall far from the tree, and I used to resent the idea that I was merely a variation on my elders. Now I find it a comfort. I am not him, and I am on the verge of becoming a father myself, which has changed the question. It is no longer what I received but what will be received from me.

My son is due in March. By the time he is old enough to hold the hammer, I will have been practising for years, and I hope I will have learned at least a little of the patience. I will not tell him what to value; actions, as the saying goes, speak louder than words. He will probably remember how I fixed things, and how I behaved when they broke, long after he has forgotten anything I said.

Time will tell what he makes of it all. The hammer is to be his, whatever he decides to build.

10.title: A letter to 2075
10.brief: Your school is burying a time capsule to be opened in fifty years. You have been chosen to give the closing speech at the ceremony. Write a speech addressed to both the present audience and those who will open the capsule.
10.briefEs: Escribe el discurso de cierre de la ceremonia de una cápsula del tiempo escolar, dirigido a los presentes y a quienes la abrirán dentro de cincuenta años.
criteria: Advanced future forms (is to be opened, will have been retired, is on the verge of, by the time).
Nuanced comparatives (the more… the more, every bit as, nowhere near as).
At least two proverbs or fixed expressions used naturally (time will tell, better late than never, history repeats itself).
A warm, memorable tone with direct address to two audiences.
10.model:
Principal, teachers, fellow students, and, in fifty years' time, whoever you are,

Good afternoon. This capsule is to be opened in the year 2075, by which time most of us standing here will have been retired for decades, and some of us, I suspect, will be grumbling about the young. So let me speak first to you, the strangers we cannot picture.

You are holding, by now, a handful of objects that must look nowhere near as impressive as whatever you carry in your pockets. A letter from each class, a mobile phone and a photograph in which we are squinting into the sun. Please do not laugh too loudly. Our ideas, we hope, were every bit as sincere as your own.

We have also put in a list of our worries and our hopes. The more we wrote, the more we noticed how much the two overlapped. We worried about the climate, and we hoped, nonetheless, to see it improve. We are on the verge of a great many changes, and none of us can say how they will turn out. Time will tell, as my grandmother always says, and she is rarely wrong.

To my fellow students: by the time this capsule is opened, we will have been out in the world for most of our lives. We will have made mistakes, changed careers and, I hope, kept at least a few of these friendships. Better late than never, as the saying goes: it is never too late to become the person we hope the capsule will find.

So, to the people of 2075, I say: look after one another. Look after the planet we are leaving you. And if you find that we got something wrong, please remember that we were doing our best with what we knew. History, after all, has a way of repeating itself, and I hope you will forgive us for repeating some of it.

Thank you.

10.title: Executive report: an ageing city, 2025–2045
10.brief: A medium-sized city's population is ageing quickly. Write an executive report for the city council assessing the implications for housing, transport and health services over the next twenty years, and recommending priorities.
10.briefEs: Escribe un informe ejecutivo para el ayuntamiento sobre el envejecimiento de la población: vivienda, transporte y salud en los próximos veinte años, y prioridades.
criteria: Report layout with headings and an impersonal tone.
Advanced future forms (is projected to have risen, will have increased, is due to open, is on the verge of).
Nuanced comparatives (the more… the more, nowhere near, every bit as, considerably more).
A fixed expression or proverb used appropriately in a formal register (time is of the essence, a stitch in time saves nine).
10.model:
Executive Report: An Ageing City, 2025–2045

Summary
This report assesses the implications of population ageing for housing, transport and health services in the city over the next twenty years. The analysis draws on census data, the regional health authority's forecasts and consultations with three residents' associations. It concludes that the city is on the verge of a demographic shift for which current plans are nowhere near adequate, and recommends three priorities.

Projections
By 2045, the proportion of residents aged over sixty-five is projected to have risen from 14 to 26 per cent. The number of people living with long-term conditions will have increased accordingly, and a smaller working-age population will be supporting a considerably larger retired one. The more the city grows older, the more demand there will be for services that are accessible, local and affordable.

Implications
Housing. Existing stock is poorly suited to older residents: fewer than one home in ten is step-free. A new sheltered housing scheme, which is due to open in 2027, will serve only a fraction of the need.
Transport. Reduced mobility makes public transport every bit as important as medical care, yet most bus stops lack seating and shelter.
Health. Primary care clinics are expected to be under strain by 2035, particularly in outlying districts. Social isolation, meanwhile, is not recorded in any budget but is arguably the most pressing concern raised in consultation.

Recommendations
It is recommended that the Council:
• adopt accessibility standards for all new housing developments from next year;
• redesign the bus network around hospitals, clinics and shopping areas;
• fund community health centres in the three districts with the oldest populations.
Time is of the essence. A stitch in time saves nine, and the cost of acting now will be considerably lower than that of responding to a crisis in 2040. By then, the decisions taken this year will have shaped the quality of life of a generation.

10.title: Review: a novel set in 2150
10.brief: A literary magazine is publishing reviews of speculative fiction. Write a review of a novel, real or imagined, set in the future. Explain its vision, evaluate its plausibility and style, and say what it suggests about the present.
10.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de una novela de ficción especulativa ambientada en el futuro: su visión, verosimilitud, estilo y lo que dice del presente.
criteria: Advanced future forms when discussing the novel's world (will have been abandoned, is on the verge of, by the time, will have kept).
Nuanced comparatives (the more… the more, nowhere near as, every bit as, a good deal more).
At least one proverb or fixed expression used naturally (time will tell, the shape of things to come).
Evaluative literary vocabulary and a clear recommendation.
10.model:
The Last Orchard: A Future That Feels Uncomfortably Close

By the time the story of 'The Last Orchard' begins, the great cities of the coast will have been abandoned for a century. The novel is set in 2150, in a highland settlement of two thousand people whose survival depends on a single apple orchard. Its heroine, Marta, a grafting specialist, is on the verge of losing it to a blight, and the plot, quiet but absorbing, follows her attempt to save it.

What impresses most is the world-building. The author does nowhere near as much explaining as most writers of her genre, and the novel is all the better for it. The more we read, the more we infer: that the old governments have gone, that barter has replaced money, that knowledge is passed on by apprenticeship. These details are never announced; they emerge in conversation, in a way that is every bit as convincing as the best passages of classic dystopian fiction.

The prose is spare and precise, though it can be a good deal too austere. Marta's emotional life, in particular, is handled with such restraint that readers may find themselves wishing for a little more warmth. The middle section, in which a rival community arrives, loses momentum, and a final twist, which I will not reveal, is perhaps more convenient than earned.

And yet the book lingers. It makes no grand claims about the shape of things to come; it asks instead what we will have kept by the time the lights go out. The orchard becomes a symbol of a more modest hope: that the things worth preserving are often small, local and slow to grow. Is such a future plausible? Time will tell, but the author's vision of survival through patience, rather than heroism, is more persuasive than most.

Recommended for readers who enjoyed the quiet intelligence of 'The Road' without its relentless bleakness, and for anyone who suspects that the future will be won, if at all, by gardeners.
